div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT HOMING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT HOMING SOCIETY.

The above Society flew their last Young Bird Race on Monday last, August 17th, from Bath 140 miles. Mr. S. Taylor convoyer travelled to Bath with the Birds on. Friday night,so as to liberate on Saturday,but after wait- ingfuntil noon, was obliged to wire home,unable to toss birds, weather dull, thick, raining. Accordingly he held them over until Monday morning, liberating them at 8.30 a.m., South wind, dull weather. At the home end it was very dull and unfavourable. Messrs. Walker 8: Sons timed in first bird at 12.48 it taking 4 hours 18 minutes. Velocity 948 yards per minute. 23 members sent 273 birds.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLAR GONVENTIOM.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLAR GONVENTIOM.

The half-yearly: session of the No: 1 Convention South West Lancashire, was held on Saturday in the Co-operative Hall, Earle street, Earlestown. Bro. J. Parr, C. 0, T. (Leigh) presided over a good muster of representatives and visitors, Warrington being particularly well represented. The 'usual committee were appointed, Bro. F. Merlin, (Warrington) acting on the . Credential Committee and Bro's Bate (Warrington) and Rose (Earlestown) on the Finance Committee. Bro. Parr, C. C. T. in his report stated that the order in the area was in a satisfactory con- dition. He was pleased to say that in all the lodges there was a bond of brotherhood and sisterhood which boded well for the future success of the lodges. The :report Of the secretary (Bro. Smith) Ashton) showed that in May there was a membership of 352, and now the membership is 359. This, how- ever, is a decrease of 17 on the February. returns. The quarter had been a recard one with regard to fraternal tyisiting between lodges. The C.S.J.T.'s (Sister Woods, Earlestown) showed a membership of 537 juveniles in eight temples. This was a decrease of 75 on the quarter, owing to one temple having. dosed with 99 members. Bro. Warburton, treasurer Earlestowia) showed a substantial balance in hand. The election of officers resulted as follows ;—c.o.T. Bro. Parr (Leigh) ; C. Conn, Bro. G. Clarke (Earles) town) ; C.S.J.T. Sister Mrs. Woods (Earlestown) , C.C.S. Bro. F. Merlin (Warrington); C.Sec., Bro. P. Smith (Ashton); C.V.T., Sister Battersby (Leigh) ; C. Treasurer, Bro. Warburton (Earlestown,; C. Chaplain, Bro. Rev. G. Cook (Earlestown) ; C. Marshall, Bro. P. Hulme (Leigh) ; P.C.C.T., Bro Lindon (St. Helens).; C.A.S., Bro. French (Bamfur-• long) ; C.D01., Sister Potter (Wigan); C.G. Bro. Bate (Warrington) ; U.S., Bro. Lewis (Widnes). The officers were installed by Bro. Morris Jones, P.G.C.T. -,(Liverpool) assisted :by Bro. Roberts (Warrington) and Sister 'Lambert (St. Heins). A public meeting was held after tea, Bro. the Rev. G. Cook presiding. A spirited address was given by Bro. Morris Jones and -an excellent programme was arranged by Sister Miss Woods, including songs, recitations, violin solos, gramaphone selections, and a selection by the War- rington Good Templar " Zobo „ Band, under the con- ductorship of Bro. A. Tanner.

div.head: DEATH OF A BOXER.
div.p: THE DEATH OF A BOXER.

On Monday- at Newcastle-on-Tyne J. Cason, an lutillery militiaman, was charged with causing the death .of J. Leach, another militiaman, in a boxing contest in Newcastle on Saturday night. A police officer gave it as his opinion that therounds were fairly contested, but in the eighth Leach fell without being struck, and on being picked up was found to be dead. The magistrates thought it a disgrace to a civilised country that the law allowed such scenes. The accused was remanded, bail being _granted. DANCED WITH A DISLOCATED .NECK.

Susannah Mackintosh, a nine-year-old girl, was play- ing on a ladder in the Tunnel Gardens, Poplar last Friday when a boy came up and pulled her by the leg and she fell on the back of her head. She got up, how- ever, and did not seem hurt, for she afterwards danced to an organ. When she went home she became ill, and died the next day. A house surgeon made the astonishing.statement at the inquest that the child's neck was dislocated by the fall, and that it must have gone back to its place, which was a most extraordinary occurrence.

div.head: CONSTIPATION CURED. Bile Beans and a Great Physician.
div.p: CONSTIPATION CURED. Bile Beans and a Great Physician.

Use of Chas. Forcle's bile beans is the safest and surest method of curing constipation ; and if the advice of so great a physician as the late Sir Andrew Clark is to be considered as having any value, this ailment will be treated ibyl sufferers asisoon as it occurs. That cele- brated physician hold that constipation was the cause of one half of the ailments from which women suffer. Some twelve months ago in Elcho Place, Bourne (Lines) a young lady named Edith Allan began to suffer from this ailment, which brought on indigestion and. headache. Her own description of her sufferings is as follows : "I had no rest day or night, as I was always in pain. Every bit of food I took settled heavilr on my chest and I felt as if I wanted to be sick and could'nt. I tried all remedies could think or hear of, but nothing did me good. As my friend says, I was like a walking chemist's shop. I consulted two doctors, took their medicine and followed their advice for three months; but still I felt worse instead of better. What little food I managed to take did me no good, and not a day passed but what I felt ill. The headaChe was terrible. At times T could scarcely crawl about in the day time, and at night I could not sleep. "The doctor said I ought to have more fresh air in- stead of being indoorsall day, so I made a change and went to stay with my brother at Leigh. That was last September. I was very bad then, and my brother advised me to try Charles Forde's bile beans,and I took' his advice. After I had been taking bile beans three weeks, I began to feel alot better; so much so, in fact, that I kept on with them until I had flveboxes. These cured me completelyaind lan now in the best of health.' Thousands of cases similar to the above could be quoted and every sufferer from constipation, indigestion, head- ache, liver complaint, and allied symptoms, should lose no time in applying this great vegetable specific. Bile beans do not merely purge, giving temporary re- Betonly, like the old-fashioned- so-called remedies of forty or fifty yearsago. They act directly on the liver and digestive organs, strengthening and stimulating those organs to perform their natural duties, so that when the medicine is left off the cure remains per- manent. Bile beans are sold by all chemists, but you are warned against useless, if -not actually harmful, sub- a° ti f utes.

div.head: OMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: OMEN'S CHAT.

IThe King's desire for rest and retirement has been I sadly ignored by spectators and visitors at Marienbad. 1 His Majesty can command most things,but the privilege of privacy which all his subjects enjoy, is denied him. IWhenlPrince of Wales, the King found it very difficult to:escape the obstrusive curiosity of the crowd, which lis generally a very mixed one at the Continental Spas, , button the present occasion the eagerness of a multitude 1 of people to press round and stare at him, has been such lan anuoyance as to interfere with the King's arrange- ments for daily exercise and recreation. His Majesty is on a private visit to Marienbad and is travelling in- coenito as the Duke of Lancaster, but the fact that the King wishes to spend his holiday as a private gentleman has no effect in checking the rudeness of many people who seize every possible occasion to crowd round and stare at him. _ _ _

The privacy which Queen Victoria enjoyed at Bal- moral,added not a little to her fondness for the Highlands. It is a very natural and human desire to go about unmo- lested and unobserved, and it is not surprising that so many members of the Royal Family prefer to spend their holidays in the Scottish Highlands. Queen Alexandra will stay at Balmoral until the end of the month, but her Majesty will spend most of the time with the Duke and Duchess of Fife, who always pass the greater part of the autumn on Deeside. Sport of all kinds is the keynote of life at Mar Lodge, where the parties are sociable, and free from formality. • The Duchess of Fife always wears, when in Scotland, toilettes of the most simple and practical type. Holi- days are nothing if they cannot be spent out of doors. and the costume that will stand all weathers should be the aim of all who desire to enjoy themselves. More- over, for holiday purposes, the smartest women are those who are most simply dressed, and nothing is better for country wear than the Norfolk coat, with a moderately short skirt and stout, well-fitting boots. The material should be warm, without being heavy, and if one has any idea of golfing, fishing, or going out with the guns it ought to be rainproof. The best Scotch, Welsh, and Irish home-spuns fulfil these requirements, and in appropriate shades, no better choice can be made for a serviceable holiday costume. The new red, a rich but not garish dye, known as "heraldry," is enjoying a wide vogue for the best travelling costumes' the skirts of which, in all instances clear the ground all round, the hem in the great majority of cases being of soft leather. This appears to the depth of about two inches on the right and four inches on the wrong side, and possesses the advantage of being quickly freed from dust and mud by means of a damp sponge. For some time past we have known ourselves to be drifting on towards the day of the long coat, and this day has now arrived. The long coat which we are all going to wear this autumn and coming winter is cut to follow the outlines of the figure without fitting them, with a narrow back, held in like the guard's coats, by a strap. In front it falls in full folds from under a deep collar. In every variety of woollen material such coats are being built, and later we shall doubtless see them in fur. That the fur coat however, even for motoring is a mistake in this cowatry,is an assured fact. It nearly always induces cold, the violent change when it is re- moved being more than ordinary lungs and chest can bear.

Many of the new long coats shew slits in the side i seams through which it s pos-sible to thrust one's hand andlso hold up therskirt beneath. These are useful, and should be insisted upon, but the skirt worn underneath a long coat should never be long enough to need holding up, save when descending stens or getting out of a vehicle ecc. Only those who have tried to walk in a long coat and long skirt, know the horrors of the situation.

It is not easy to perceive the practical advantage of!the information tabulated by a government department with reference to the mean age at marriage of men and women respectively married during the last ten quinquennial periods. Speaking roughly, the mean appears to have been about 28 in the case of men, and 2G in the case of women, but these figures do not afford the least inform- ation ase,to the age at which the majority marry. While there are on the one hand thousands. of impro- vident marriages of mere children, many others marry at an advanced age. There is on the register at Green- wich Parish Church, the record of a marriage between a man named Cooper, %god 108, to a woman 88. That wedding would tend to raise the average for that particu- lar church, but it would not afford any criterion of the age at which people generally married in that parish. Besides many clergymen have perniitted the parties, when they were obviously of riper years, to enter , themselves as of " full age,' and although the suggestion is a mere speculation, yet it is possible that that des- cription is applied to more people of advanced years than to couples in the twenties. The introduction of the automobile baby carriage. which has already made its appearance in the streets of , Paris, will be regarded as a fresh aggravation by the non-motoring public. The baby carriage, even though it is so much lighter and more graceful than the old- fashioned perambulator, is regarded by some people as at all times a nuisance on the pavements, but with an engine attached to its wheels, it will become a source af \t, still greater annoyance to hem. One however can hardly regard the motor basi tte very seriously, or anything more than another syn tom of "motor mad- ness," whioh perhaps pictures the -rising generation 1 driving their own motor prams along theitreets. But ! its thumping and shaking could scarcely be good for the ; child, and it is not likely that any nursemaid would be allowed to bring this new "terror'," on the pavements. A licence is required for keeping a man servant, but now that many men do the work of housemaids, the question arises whether ;the licence, which costs 15s. a year, ought not to be abolished. A London householder • who was summoned on this .score, declared that the j man servant in question was his 'housemaid," and it j is said at the servants' registries that a large number of ! men, mostly foreigners, are employed in private and ! boarding houses to do the housework, and that they do it better and quicker than is ordinarily the case with women servants. One however can scarcely look to a development of this movement for the solution of the , great servant problem, though those who try it should I certainly be relieved of any liability to be summoned 1 by the Inland Revenue authorities.
MADGE.

div.head: MR. CARNEGIE AND THE ST. HELENS LIBRARIES.
div.p: MR. CARNEGIE AND THE ST. HELENS LIBRARIES.
Gift of £6,000.

At the meeting of the St. Helens Free Libraries Com- mittee, on Wednesday, Councillor H. Martin, who occu- pied the chair in the absence of the chairman (Mr. H. R. Lacey), said that twelve months ago the question of a new branch library at Sutton was raised, and also the desirability of a new branch library being established for the Newtown district...Et was felt by the members of the committee that the time had come when they might take advantage of Mr. Carnegie's generosity by asking him to contribute towards building the two branch libraries. The Committee, after consultation with the then Mayor (Colonel W. W. Pilkington) and Sir David Gamble, sent a letter to Mr. Carnegie, placing before him the requirements of the borough of St. Helens. Mr. Carnegie promised to give £3,000 to each of the branch library buildings at Sutton and Newtown, provided that sites be given them, the cost of same not being a burden upon the library rate,and provided also that an increased rate be imposed suffici- ent to maintain those libraries at a cost of not less than £2OO per year each. The offer of Mr. Carnegie was accepted, and it was decided that Lieutenant-Colonel W. Lee Pilkington, the landowner, be. approached with reference to the Sutton site, and that Mr. Robinson be approached with reference to the Newtown site, the winner of which is Sir Gilbert Greenall.
FLOUR THE BEST'. IT ISI
FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Blouses are very much in evidence, for not only has every woman proved their value as a useful article of dress but never before have they attained to such a degree of elegance and general daintiness. Very fine lawn and Valenciennes lace trimmed and inserted blouses are worn by way of contrast with coarse crash or linen costumes, while with serge gowns embroidered linen shirts are correct wear. One of the latest fads for giving- a finish to a cambric shirt is the addition of a Toby frill of finely pleated
MART BLOUSE.

cambric, similarly pleated cambric frills being worn at the wrists. Very delightful and cool to wear are' the Tussore silk blouses which not only wear well but clean beautifully. Tussore silk is at once pliable and soft, and tucks well. It falls if gathered into the most graceful folds and is one of the few fashionable materials which appears at its best when smocked. Lace and embroidery enhance still further its charms, and a very charming blouse I recently admired had its shaped collar enhanced by the embroidery thereon of a spray of beautifully embroidered flowers and leaves, the colours being chosen to imitate nature as faithfully as possible. A decorative touch such as this which goes so far to increase the beauty and value of the garment is one which most girls could easily work at home in their leisure moments, and the time thus spent would be well repaid by the distinction thus conferred on the blouse.

The smart blouse given in my sketch is designed for seaside wear and is of Tussore silk which, as I stated, has become quite the rage of the season. The wide collar is tucked and finished at the lower edge by a handsome silk fringe. A dainty little turn- over collar of lace finished the throat, while a bow and ends of foulard silk is carelessly

div.head: WHOLE CLOTH • COSTUMEJ
div.p: A WHOLE CLOTH • COSTUMEJ

knotted in front. The , loose easily-fitting sleeves are caught at the wrists into a lace band. Lace, as we all know, is the trimming par excellence on all items of dress, and among the first and foremost varieties are Irish filet, Cluny Valenciennes, Chantilly, Mechlin, and sc me less generally known which are made in some of the convents in South -.America. Other trimmings, how- ever, besides lace are in great demand, and are often used to contrast or intermingle with the lace used as insertions or as motifs. Braids for serge or cloth costumes are much in vogue and are of all descrip- .tions—silk, wool, chenille or soutache, and in plain or mixed colours. Then the old- fashioned smocking or crochet in coloured silks are fashionable, and embroideries in silk or drawn threads darned into an artistic design. In short, anyone who has a taste for needlework can use many otherwise wasted half-hours in beautifying her gowns. The white cloth costume depicted is altogether a la mode. It is trimmed with narrow waved gold cord on both coat and skirt, and is further enhanced by machine stitchings which appear in lines on the lower edge of the cape-like collar and the turned- back reveres. The bolero is cut up at each side, and although it pinches slightly at the

div.head: SIMPLE HAT:
div.p: A SIMPLE HAT:

back it is caught into a shaped band, for this mode is newer than the loose-backed style. Indeed the smartest cloth or serge bolero is that in which the blouse pleated effect of the upper part is retained while the lower part is banded into a deep shaped band which gives a trim, neat appearance to the waist. , Sometimes as a variety or relief to the some- what wearying monotony of the bolero triple capes of the same material as the skirt worn are substituted. These have armholes through which the arms can be slipped, which not I only peritiit of greater liberty of movement I but keep the capes in place some, indeed, even possess sleeves. These pretty little capes which are exceedingly chic if well cut, and which come to a few inches of the waistband, can be worn open or closed right up. They admirably serve the purpose of ; establishing continuity between the lower and upper part of the toilette. This simple hat is suited for travelling wear as it is neat and trim, and the brim keeps the veil usually worn on such occasions well out from the face. It is made solely of fancifully pleated straw and owes its success to its shape which is comfortable to wear and smart to look at. There are many novelties in the realms of millinery', and amongst the most sensible of thise are the new yachting caps of tussore silk, which are made with a fuller crown than of yore which partakes more of the beefeater, and although not so trim as the shape to which we are accustomed is more becoming. These hats are delight- fully cool and light to wear. The Breton sailor hat still holds its own in popularity, and indeed one might condense the many modes into three which are distinctly pre-eminent, namely, the plateau, the FrenCli sailor, and the mushroomi Cogunrriti

div.p: CHAPTER XVII.
WALROYD HEARS AN ECHO FROM THE PAST.

THE morning after Emrys Tredegar's escape four policemen came up to the Plas Tredegar to take the prisoner to Cardigan jail. A sergeant was shown into Walroyd's study, and asked for the key of the cellar. Walroyd unlocked a small drawer in his writing table and taking out the key, handed it to the man. "I think I will come down with you," he said.. He preferred to face the situation in the semi-darkness rather than in the full light of day. _ _

When they unlocked the door and found that the bird had flown, no one appeared more astounded and furious than John T. Walroyd. He swore loudly and denounced the police as incompetent duffers. He sent for the servants and accused them one after the other of abetting the prisoner's escape. He went back to- his study and examined the lock of the drawer with a magnifying glass to see if it had been tampered with in the night. He theorised and cross questioned and abused till the police thought he must have had a personal spite against Tredegar. Finally he sent three of them off to rouse the whole neighbourhood to a general hunt, and took the sergeant into his study. "Someone in the house has a duplicate of that key," he said sternly. "It is your duty to find it, sergeant. I give you a free your The sergeant laughed apologetically. "Excuse me, sir," he said, "but it has occurred to me that there may be some secret way out of the cellar, known to Mr. Tredegar. It is an old house, and I have heard of such things—stones that move when you press a knob and such like."
"What about the handcuffs," Walroyd replied contemptously. "They have been unlocked."

"Very true," the man said, "but they may have been unlocked before he was shut up. He might have been furnished with a key. It would be easy to keep the handcuffs in their place. Then he could unfasten the chains off his ankles."

"Incredible," said Walroyd. "Have you ever read the story of Jack Shepherd, sir," the sergeant asked. " Won- derful things do happen." "Well, go and look," Walroyd replied sharply, "and mark you, Evans, I shall not consider myself 'responsible for this escape. There has been some carelessness some Where. And it is a scandalous thing that there is no prison house in a village of this size. Good morning." "I suppose no one could have got that key of yours, sit." Impossible. The key of this drawer is always on my chain. The lock has not been tampered with. You can inspect it your- self.'

The sergeant inspected the lock, and then left the room. He made things very un- pleasant in the house. for a whole hour. Even the guests were subjected to a thorough cross- examination. Mavanwy almost broke down under, the strain. It was well known that Tredegar was her lover, and Sergeant Evans did not spare her feelings. Cynthia alone was calm and collected. Her answers were enough to chill the , ardour of the most en- thusiastic detective. The sergeant left her with profuse apologies. But before he left he had a private Word with Mr. Morgan and hinted that it would be the duty of the police to watch :f.,lynglas. Hue and cry was raised over the whole country side, and that very evening a -gigantic form resembling Emrys Tredegar was seen by three sailors in the LlVneas woods. It evaded the pursuit, however, and disappeared on the bog of. Gogerddan. But its appear- ance was sufficient to confine the chase to the immediate neighbourhood of Garth. Cynthia Cantrip and her father left the Plas Tredegar after lunch. When he heard the news of his (laughter's engagement, he chuckled, and blessed heaven for having so favoured his plans. His small keen mind saw through the whole business to the very core, and he blessed Emrys Tredegar and even hoped that he would escape from his pursuers. He. put two and two together and realised that .Tredegar's escape and Cynthia's en- gagement were not entirely unconnected. When Cynthia arrived home at their lodgings, shi went upstairs to her room, and lay down on her bed. Her head ached as though it would .split. Her mind circled dizzily through the events of the last twenty- four hours, and they spun past her like an endless shower of meteors. Among them in its turn came the incident of the half disc she had seen on Walroyd's writing table. She had not till then given it a second thought. Other and more important matters had crowded it from her brain. She rose from her her bed, and, unlocking a drawer, took out her jewel case. One by one she drew out its sparkling contents till she came to the last tray. Then she lifted that, and there lay the half disc. She started back in surprise. She had only looked for it as a matter of form, for she could have sworn that it was in the possession of John Walroyd. But it as still in her jewel case, and it was absolutely impossible that he could have replaced it. She gazed at it stupidly, as though it had been some strange apparition that she could not understand. Then slowly the truth began to dawn upon her. She recollected that there had been no chain on the one she had seen on Walroyd's table, and, as far as she could remember, there had not even been a hole by which it might have been attached to anything, but she could not be positive on this latter point. The truth, however, grew clearer and clearer, as she recalled the details. It was quite evident that the piece of gold she had seen the night before was the other half of the Jim Her brain reeled, as she tried to grasp this extraordinary coincidence, and to trace some connection between the owners of the two halves. But she could .arrive at no definite conclusion. A hundred impossible ideas rose up before her, and vanished like ghosts before the breath of reason. Only one thing was clear in all her thoughts—the face of her dead husband. She resolved, however, to learn as much of the truth as John Walroyd would tell her, or she could gather from a careful scrutiny of his face. The very next afternoon she had - promised to walk with him along the rocks. It was their first walk as acknowledged lovers, and she had looked forward to it with dread. But now she regarded it in a favourable light. She put the half disc in her pocket. and closing her jewel case, she put it in t'ab drawer. At r 0.30 on the following morning John Walrovd called. His face was radiant with triumph. The whole village knew by now that he was engaged to Cynthia Cantrip,cand even the children regarded him in a new light as he strode down the street. Cynthia was ready to go out when he arrived at the door. She met him in the passage, and gave him no opporturay of entering their sitting-room or indulging in any demonstration of affection. But the warm, strong clasp of his hand told her plainly that he longed to take her in his arms. They walked down the street together, and were the cynosure of every eye. .The sailors lounging at their doorways grinned and spat contemplatively. as they passed. The village girls nudged each other and winked. One old woman was sitting on her doorstep, under the mystic sign of " Temperance " which was inscrined on the lintel, apparently to show that the sweets and bootlaces within were not intoxicating. She waved a withered hand to them, and mumbled some kindly blessing in Welsh. Cynthia felt as though she could sink into the ground with shame. It seemed like smile cheap exhibition of herself before the common people, It was an indignity and

_ •tureo Anoapad sem pAoilum uu two angry glances at him. She felt like some captive woman led before the chariot of her conqueror. At last she could stand it no longer. "Let us go on the beach," she said. is so dusty here, and my head aches." " Certainly, dear," Walrovd answered " But the tide has only just • left the sands, and they are rather wet. " I prefer the wet to this dust," she said ; "and the houses keep off the little breeze there is"
" It

They turned down a narrow passage be- tween two cottages and crossed the shingle on to the sand. They cut across this to where the long reefs and plateaux of rock ran out from the cliffs into the water. and the wet seaweed glistened in the sunlight, The sand oozed under their boots as they walked. Here and there they passed through little rivulets still flowing down from the wet shingle above, and the water splashed up under their feet.

Walroyd talked to Cynthia in quiet, even tones that gave no indication of the passionate nature of his thoughts. He spoke of general subjects. and touched on most of them in a spirit of cynical humour. Cynthia listened, and hardly answered him. But occasionally she laughed at some remark he made.

Every now and then : she would stop and pick up some shell from the sand. Shells had always fascinated Cynthia Cantrip, and on this particular day she sympathised with them. They had been cast, like human lives, out of the calm, deep ' security of the sea to lie on the beach beneath the scorching scrutiny of the sun. Some wore unharmed, some were divided from their twin mate and lay disconsolate, and some—were broken. At last they reached the rocks, and began - to scramble over them towards the shore. Some were sharp and jagged and covered with limpets, while others lay buried a foot.. deep under the tangled masses of slippery weed. Among them 'lay clear, deep pools bright with anemones and waving fronds of green and crimson. Progress was, difficult, and it was necessary for Cynthia to hold Walroyd's hand. She almost wished that she had con,: tinned along the road and then taken to the beach where the cliffs began to rise and curve round to the West.

At last they reached the shingle, and Wal- royd suggested that they should 'it down under a tall, detached piece of rock. The tides had hollowed out the base of it into a smooth curve, which just fitted the lines of the human ,body. It was a spOt much fav- oured by lovers; but Cynthia, who was almost a stranger to the neighbourhood, did not know that. She saw, however, that it was a very secluded place, and that the rock shut off all view of the village of Garth, where there were many telescopes and keen eyes. She shrank from it instinctively. Then she smiled. She had sold herself, and had no right to refuse to carry out her bargain. She was the betrothed wife of John Walroyd. They sat down under the shadow of the rock, and gazed out across the sea. Wal- royd made no demonstration of affection. He had began to realise that Cynthia re- garded him as. a stranger, even if she did not actually dislike him. .He could afford to bide his time.

It was a glorious morning, and two lovers might have revelled in the sunshine and the quiet of it all. The sea, blue and smooth, rippled silently to the sands, or gurgled gently as it swayed against the long line of rocks. A hot autumn haze hung over the distant circle of hills. and . suggested 'pos- sibilities of Alpine heights beyond. Across the bar of the distant estuary lay a thin, white line of foam.. Nothing moved but the sea and two oyster-catchers running lightly over the rocks in search of food. The sky above was cloudless. A faint breeze came sighing across the waters, and stirred a few pieces of dry seaweed lying on the shore. But neither Walroyd nor Cynthia saw aught of the beauty of this peaceful scene. One had no thoughts for anything but the lovely woman by his side. To the other the very quiet of the place seemed but a mockery of the tumult in her own heart, and her subtle brain was turning over half a dozen schemes for breaking off her engagement without going • back from her plighted word. For two or three minutes both were silent. Cynthia stirred the pebbles with her fingers as though searching for something. Wal- royd did not look at her, but his fingers closed quietly over one di her hands. She .did not withdraw it from his clasp. It was part of the price she had to pay. Then she looked at him in the face and sud- denly turned her head away. "I have something to tell you," she said, in a hesitating voice. " Something I ought to have 'told you last night. I do not think you will misjudge me, and say that I obtained Tredegar's release under false pretences." " What is it, dear ?" he said, gently; but at the same time • he shot a quick glance of mistrust at her from under his dark eyebrows, and the grip of his fingers tightened On her hand. " I should have told you last night," she repeated. "but .my mind was filled with so much else ; and, after all, it will not matter much." She paused,. and looked nervously round, as though she fancied that someone might be listening. "Well. Cynthia ?-" he said. "I hardly know how to tell you," she fal- tered. " I am so afraid you will be angry." He smiled reassuringly, as though such a thing were impossible. • " Well," she continued, " in plain. words, I am an impostor! I am supposed to be a single woman. As a matter of . fact, I am a widow. I was married .more than eight years ago. I had very good reasons for dropping my husband's name. It was. no credit to anyone, I assure you." Walroyd received the news wth perfect equanimity. It was no shock to him that this woman had had another husband. He had no love for the innocence of a girl.: But he was determined to hear the truth. "Look me in the face, Cynthia," he said, still holding her hand. She turned, and her frank face met his keen look of enquiry. " You are telling me the truth ?" he asked. quietly. "This is no fiction, invented in the hope that I shall release you from your word ?" She flushed indignantly. Yet part of the accusation was true. She did hope that he would break off their engagement, and that is why she told him the truth. " It is all true," she replied. "Did you divorce your husband ?" he asked. "No," she answered, bitterly; " he divorced himself. He left me to starve—in America ?" - "In America ? " "Yes. He subsequently went into part- nership in a pawnbroker's business with two other menbrotliers, I believe. Then all three sailed for South America. The ship was lost at sea." Walroyd started. But as Cynthia looked round at him, his face grew hard and inscrut- able, as a stone sphinx. But she could feel his hand tremble, and the grip seemed to tighten. on hr fingers. • He is dead, then ?" Walroyd asked, in • an even voice, "He is supposed to be dead," she an- swered. "There were only two survivors of the wreck, and they, curiously enough. were his two partners. I was in America when they were brought back to England

by the ship that picked them up. I read the story in the papers, and at once tried to communicate with them. But they had dis- appeared, and all trace of them was lost in London. It was, however, clear from theis narrative, which .they told at some length to the- reporters. that they were the only survivors, and that they had seen the others perish with their own eyes." "It is, then, certain that your husband is dead ?" Walroyd asked. "He will not return, like Enoch Arden, and find you married to another man."
"He will not return," she answered, slowly. She was thinking of the broken piece of chain that Tredegar said that he had found on a dead man's wrist. She dared not speak of it to Walroyd.

"He will not return," she repeated. " But I thought I ought ,to tell you all this in case—in case—anything did happen." "You are quite right to tell me, Cynthia," he replied. "Quite right. I will make eoquiries, though as it happened so long ago I am afraid it will be difficult to trace the survivors you spoke of. What was the name of the ship ?"
"The ' Wisahickon.' " "And the name of your husband your name ?" " Heatherbutt." • "And the name of the survivors ?"

"Peterson—Henry and William Peterson." Walroyd made notes on a piece of paper. Then he turned away from Cynthia, . and -Looked out across the sea. His face was an impenetrable mask. But one of the muscles of his upper lip twitched slightly, and if Cynthia could have seen into his dark eyes she would have gazed through them as through windows, into the blazing hell of his soul.
CHAPTER XVIII
WILLIAM PETERSON, PAWNBROKER.

THEY stayed for but a short time under the rock, and to 'Cynthia's intense relief Walroycl did not again make love to her, either in word, or look, or act. He seemed pre-occupied, and absorbed in thoughts that were evidently not pleasant. She ascribed this to her crfession about her previous mar- riage, and secretly hoped that he would eventually release her from her engagement.

As thely reached the village street' they saw signs of an unusual excitement. Little groups of women stood about, vociferating noisily in Welsh. It was noticeable, how- ever, that there were no men to be seen. Even the placid sailors had disappeared from their doorsteps. Cynthia was seized with a sudden fear. She thought it possible that Tredegar had been captured. As they neared the first group of chatterers three women ran up to meet them, all speak- ing and gesticulating at once. Out of the chaos of words Walroyd. and Cynthia gathered the horrible news. Mr. Morgan had been found in d dying condition, by the path just under the Tredegar woods, and he had since expired, and his daughtet Mavanwy had disappeared. Walroyd brushed them aside. He did not wait to hear the details. _

"I will see yOu. home, Cynthia," he said, sternly, "and then I must give what help I can. Mr. Morgan and his daughter left my house seven o'clock last night, intending to walk to Llynglas. It is curious that this should have happened directly after Tre- degar's release." • Very curious," she said, gently. "But it is hardly likely that he would harm the woman he loves or kill her father."

"A man may do anything if he has lost his reason," replied Walroyd. "I am afraid I have committed a great crime on society in letting him loose. Yet there is no crime I would not commit—to win your love I" "He was innocent I" she cried, indig- nantly. "I know that Tredegar ' has had nothing to do with this or with t 4 previous murders. And you know it, too, in your heart of hearts. If he was mad, why should he have spared your life. He has no reason to lave you." "Madness comes in fits and starts," he said, doggedly. "A man may be sane one minute, and the next a raging lunatic. I fear I am responsible for Mr. Morgan's death." "You will learn the truth some day," she replied; and did not speak another word until they reached her lodgings. Walroyd _left her at the door with a mere shake of the hand and a somewhat curt "good-night." Then he made his way quickly up the village to the Plas Tredegar. Directly he left Cynthia the mask fell from his face. The lines deepened on his brow and about the corners/ of his mouth. H'e clenched his hands as he walked, and his whole appearance was that of a man whose soul was undergoing a great agony, and whose judgment wavers as to the course it should pursue. Yet his mind was far away from present events. He was not thinking of the awful tr4edy which had just taken place. For all the time a devil walked by his side and whispered to him of the past, and he could not silence its voice. c

When he reached home he found the women servants white with terror, and unable to make intelligible replies to his hurried ques- tions. The footman arid butler were out with the other men of the village. He sum- moned one of the grooms and cross-ques- tioned him. He learnt that at twelve o'clock that morning Mr. Morgan's body had been found in a ditch by the path across the bog, just where the Tredegar woods came to an end and the hillside opened out into fields of grass. He was still alive when found, and had been brought up to the Plas Tredegar, which was the nearest house. The doctor had taken the responsibility of ordering this to be done. He had tried to restore the un- fortunate man to consciousness, but Mr. Morgan died in less than an hour after he had been brought in to the house. "And Miss Morgan ?" Walroyd asked. "A messenger was sent over to Llynglas at once," the man replied. "She had not returned the night before. The servant at the house, sir, thought that both she and her father were staying another night here. I do not think any trace of her has been found at present. But they are searching every inch of the neighbourhood, and I expect they will come across the—come across her, and he shuddered. "Get a gun," said Walroyd, sharply, "anti wait for me. You can shoot, can't you ?" • " Yes, sir, a bit." "Very well. In an hour's time be waiting for me at the front door. • Have they hunted the woods round the house ? " "The first place, sir; though not more than half a dozen would go into them." " Pshaw, the foots ! " Walroyd said, angrily. "We will go through them again, Martin You aren't afraid, are you ?" The man laughed. " I ain't afraid, sir," he said ; ghosts, at any rate." "You need be afraid of nothing if you can keep your head and shoot straight.' Walroyd turned on his heel and went intc the house. Then he rang, the bell of the smoking-room. A white-faced maid entered. "Send Mrs. Davis to me," he said; "and tell her to waste no time."
"not oi

. Ina few minutes the housekeeper came in. Her eyelids were red as though she had been crying. ".Where is Mr. Morgan ?" asked W4royd. "In the big Red Room, sir," she answered, fain tl y. "Thank you, Mrs. Davis," he said. "That is all I want to know. I am going up to looli at him"

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 22, 1903.
STOCKTON HEATH GARDEN SOCIETY,

Annual Show. THE BETTER WAY. The interior of the Church Room at Stockton Heath I looked at its best on Saturday afternoon, when it was , the scene of the second annual show in connection with the Garden Society. The air was fragrant with sweet- smelling flowers, and all around were choice specimens of flowers and plants, some sent from the spacious gardens of the rich, others from the villa gardens of the middle-class, and a number from the gardens of the humble cottager. Since the inauguration of the Garden Society two years ago, an appreciable improvement has been noticeable in the cultivation of flowers in the neighbourhood, and this is due to a large extent to the healthy rivalry which the Garden Society has encouraged. Not only are prizes given for the best collections exhibited at the Society's annual show, but there are special awards for the best stocked gardens and greenhouses and the best arranged window boxes. The result ha 's been that Stockton Heath has now some of the prettiest gardens in the district, and a few of the cottage gardens are unequalled. An evidence of the additional interest taken in the society and its work was the large increase in the number of exhibits at the show on Saturday. Whereas only 56 were entered at the first show a year ago, there were no fewer than 154 at this year's show. The exhibition of flowers were of a high order, but very little fruit was shown, and this was due to the bad season which has been experienced. The vegetables were also meagre in quantity and poor in quality, but better results may be hoped for in years to come. Of the flower exhibits, sweet peas, carnations, dahlias, begonias and roses were very good but stocks were poor. A number of choice bouquets of wild flawers were also shown and greatly admired. In addition to the exhibits, a large number of flowers and plants had been sent by a number of ladies and gentlemen. These collections were "not for competition," but they pro- duced a splendid effect in the hall and heightened the attractiveness of the exhibition. A superb collection of plants in pyramid form occupied the centre of the room and these had been sent by Mr. Lyon, of Appleton Hall, and were greatly admired. Mr. Vero B. Davies, president of the society, contributed ahighly creditable display of cut flowers including sweet peas, seedling violas and pansies. Another attractive table of flowers was provided by Mr. Leonard Davies. A beautiful basket of roses and stocks formed the centre, and surrounding were some vases of mixed Wants and cut flowers, including dahlias, roses, sweet peas and phlox. Mr. Tandy showed some greenhouse plants and cut flowers, including a box of cut roses, together with carnations, dahlias, white marguerites and asters. Mr. R. T. Wynne-Jones had a table of begonias and carna- tions. Mr. Ed. Vernon also had a small table of mixed geraniums and cut flowers, while Mr. Frank Acton hada display of mixed plants. On the platform a fine collec- tion of greenhouse plants, lent by Mrs. Massey, of Acton Grange, was displayed. The collection included some beautiful maidenhair ferns and lilies. An ind ia- rubber plant, in fine condition, lent by Mr. George Whitfield was also on the platform and attracted much attention. Mr. J. Cartwright, Lower Walton, also sent some greenhouse plants, including a pot of white campanula. Mr. A. Broady sent cut flowers; Mr. H. Pearson; roses; Mrs. W. H. Woodcock and Mr. Charles Plinston, cut flowers.
B GERDA GRASS, Author of "Phil Hawcroft's Son," "The Colonel's Little Boy," "The Way of a Woman," &o.

_ "I wonder if this work of hers in the slums is more than a pose, a pretty affectation ? " mused the Rev. Ambrose Power at his writing-desk. "Those soft brown eyes she has are the exact colour of hee father's, and a more selfish, more silky, morr cold-blooded man, I'll venture, never trod shoes leather. And those,sweet ways of hers, half-shy- half-trustful—of course they're mere clever trick, of coquetry. We impecunious curate's are con- sidered fair game, I fancy, by these elegant young ladies. Not that lam so very impecunious, to be sure, but "—with a shrug of his shoulders—" so far as the daughter of Mr. Delling is concerned I am a hopeless ineligible 'indeed. It is perfectly safe to flirt with me. I could not have the effrontery to take it seriously." But his scornful lips quivered suddenly and softened, his grey eyes darkened, his fine face grew infinitely tender. _ _ _

"Oh, why do I try to cure myself," he said, aloud, "by these disloyal thoughts? Because she is a star out of my sphere, must I try to blur her brightness? She is all she seems—a dear, sweet, unaffected, noble girl. But," he ended, taking up his quill abruptly, "she is more in my thoughts than is good for me. I will answer this letter of hers about the Play Guild, and then—think of something else." The letter finished, he took it up and looked it over, half-amused, half-dismayed. _ _ _

"Looks a bit shaky, eh ? Bah! What a fool I am! She'll never think of it. I've no time to write another. I must go and see old Widow Bell, poor broken derelict, and, oh! as many of them as I can. What a Christmas some of these poor souls will have! If there were a few more helpers like Miss Delling we -might get some of these awful places cleaned up by the Day of Judgment. Well, well! This Play Guild idea of hers is very good. It has answered splendidly in some parts of London. I don't see why it shouldn't answer Here. What a marvellous girl she is She seems be as much in the swim as anybody, and yet she has always time to think out schemes of this sort."

He pocketed his letter, and getting up strode out of the room:into the hall, snatched his hat from its peg, clapped it on, and, with more energy than grace, swung himself out into the street. At the corner he posted the letter. - His way took him into the town, and, walking rapidly along the electric-lighted pavement he found himself suddenly face to face with Miss Linda Delling—the queen of his foolish heart! A shop-assistant was carrying small parcels into her carriage. With eyes beaming radiantly through her black, chenille-spotted veil she came towards Ambrose with outstretched hand.

Despite the continuous downpour of rain on Saturday afternoon there was a large attendance at the opening ceremony. In the absence of Lady Greenall. this duty devolved upon Mr. Vere B. Davies, the president. He was accompanied on the platform by the committee and officers of the society, prominent among whom was Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, who woyked indefatigal ly for the success of the show. He was ably assisted by Mr. M. G. Hearne, the assistant secretary. The (duties of treasurer were faithfully discharged by Mr. T. R. Westbrook.
1"Oh, Mr, Power," she cried, delightedly, "I have been wishing to see you. I have something to shew you." She took a folded paper from her muff and flourished it before him.

The President, hi declaring the show open, said Lady Greenall asked him specially- to apologise for her absence and to say how greatly interested she was in the society and that she hoped it would be a success. He thought he ought also to apologise for himself for he felt that a gentleman was a very poor substitute for a lady. (Laughter.) Then he must alsd apologise for the weather, or the Clerk of the Weather ought to apologise to them. (Hear, hear.) The rain • they had had, had affected some of the flowers very • considerably but he thought they would all agree 6 havin"regard to the amount of rain they had had within the last few days—that the show was a very creditable one. (Hear, hear.) A society of that description was worthy of the utmost support, because it tended to encourage the working °lasses to take a pride in their, gardens and to brighten their homes. He wished it every success, and hoped they would have better luck in , future years as regarded the weather. The Rev. H. V. Pigot,in proposing a vote of thanks to the Presidentand officers of the society,said Mr. Davies was a very appropriate gentleman to be at the head of a great movement of that sort, and he (Mr. Pigot) felt relieved last year when he relinquishei the office for Mr. Davies. They were indebted to him for the in. terest he had shown in the society and the enthusiasm he had displayed, for he had been a regular attender at the society's meetings, and a most efficient president, • Mr. Jenkins' work as secretary was well known, as was also that of the treasurer, Mr. T. R. Westbrook. They also had a strong and sensible committee, The society had made mistakes, but in time they hoped to draw up a schedule which would exactly suit the district. Had the summer been a little kinder and given them more sunshine and a little less rain they would have had a wonderful display that day, as the interest taken in the growing of flowers in the -district was phenomenal. Mr. E. J. Hall seconded the vote of thanks, and said that considering the difficulties they had experienced, the display of flowers was surprising and excited their 'admiration. By no means the least pleasant part of the ; society's work was seen from week to week in the wonderful improvements which had been made in the gardens in the village since the societyhad been formed. • Their sense of gratitude to the society for making the district blossom like the rose could not be expressed by the'resolution he now submitted. (Hear, hear.) The vote of thanks having been passed, the President, in reply, said the society seemed to be making good progress, as the number of exhibits had increased from 56 to 154. Thanks were also accorded to Mrs; Pigot and Mrs. Vere Davies, who judged the table decorations; Messrs. Parker and Parkinson who judged the outdoor exhibits; and Messrs. Lockhart and Calder, who judged the ' general exhibits. Some appreciative remarks were also made with regard to the musical entertainment, which was given during the afternoon by the Misses Bouchier (piano and violin), and Miss G. Ball, who rendered several songs with taste and skill. I Miss Edgerley dispensed an enjoyable tea to the officials and friends of the society.
He took it and opened its. In sprawling hiero- glyphics was written:
- "iI hereby sertifies that i will not tech strong tickers no more.—Yours truly, ROBERT JIM."
Ambrose handed back the document.

"I am very glad for Jugg, Miss Dolling," he said, a little sadly, "and very sorry for myself. What is it I am wanting in? Tell me the secret of your success. I have been at this same poor Jugg—oh, times without number. And Jugg has politely informed me-- But I am keeping you ? " _ _

"No, no, indeed. lam most glad to have met you, if only to wish you a happy Christmas when it comes. And, oh! would you mind giving this "—a soft gloved hand stole into his and left a coin—"to poor Mrs. Jugg. Her husband was in all the time, and I'm afraid my faith in him has not got backbone yet. So I dared not give her anything before him. Oh, did you get my letter? Have you found me any children for my Play Guild? "I have scores for you, Miss Delling." "Oh ! " She gave a pretty start of assumed alarm. "I hope we shall be equal to them all, poor little things. Thank you very much for getting me such a nice large room, piano and all. It will do splendidly, and I have got a lovely Christmas-tree for it already. lam going away to-morrow for a fortnight's visit to some friends, but I shall be at liberty at once when I come back. My father is going to Nice, by the way. He detests our English Christmas. Isn't it odd? I love it. And now, good-bye. I hope you will have a very happy holiday." So with mutual good wishes they parted.

"A happy Christmas for me said the Rev. Ambrose, gloomily, in the privacy of his heart. "Ah, that is very likely! Perhaps—if I had never met Linda Delling. But now the best will always be wanting. I hope she will meet her fate this holiday. I wish she would get married. I should have to forget her then. Jugg is more in her thoughts than I am." It was a cloudy night, with promise of snow. Not a star was to be seen. Coming out from the lively, brilliantly-lit streets straight into utter gloom and solitude Ambrose Power crossed over, and, opening the railway gates, passed over the row of lines that divided prosperous, respectable Port Rushborough with its glittering shops, its fine houses, its pretty ladies and elegant gentlemen, from the collection of slums known as the Old Town. Here, amid the murkiness and filth, amid the noise of coarse laughter and quarrelsome oaths, a barrel-organ was grinding out the last strains of "Ora Pro Nobis." Close upon Piccolomini's solemn melody came the frolicsome trills and runs of a gay, new-fangled dance. Tattered little girls left their corners swiftly, chose other tattered little girls for partners, came out into the middle of the road, and there stood waiting with nodding heads to catch the time, and then began to dance. Merrily their rags danced too. Ambrose stood and watched them with a tender pity, heedless of the whispered jeers about him, till leisurely a police- man sauntered up and waved a hand majestically Without a murmur the crowd of little dancer. melted away. The "bobby" was part of the programme. "For its size," mused Ambrose, as he picked his way, "Port Rushborough has managed to collect a marvellous lot of vice and filth, and— organ-grinders. One finds these dancing groups in every little dirty street, and always an ogre in blue pouncing down on their fun. I suppose this is what has made her think of a Play Guild. Poor little souls! They need a refuge for their harmless frolics badly."

Drumming his taper fingers impatiently upon a small table beside him, Mr. Delling looked out upon his spacious grounds, covered now with some inches of snow, and, with a rare moodiness in his handsome, velvety brown eyes, awaited the home-% coming of his only daughter, Linda, from her fortnight's Christmas visit in the country. "It's odd!" he mused. "Linda and I have been the best of friends always, and yet—l don't know her in the least. I haven't the faintest notion how she will take it. H'm 1'

He began to pace the beautiful room fretfully, and then, with a sudden return of his ordinary philosophical calm, he sat down at the keyboard of the grand piano and began to weave soft, dreamy melodies that were reminiscent of bits of Verdi and Mascagni, but which he was placidly convinced were quite his own. Fascinating beyond description—for what pen could tell how mellow was his voice, how winning were his ways ?—gallant with women, cordial with men, Geoffrey Delling was yet, in his sixtieth year, the idol of Port Rushborough's mushroom society. But little above the middle height, he was inclined, though quite becomingly, to the plumpness of good living and an indulgent • con- science. Brows and moustache still wore their original hue, but his raven hair had rapidly turned snow-white. Thick and fine and wavy it had, how- ever, suffered no loss of beauty from the change, and his soft brown eyes but shone the darker for the contrast. He had an effective tenor voice, was a delightful dancer, a very fair artist in water- colours—behold his moonlight scenes and storm- tosded vessels here upon the richly-papered walls— he was devoted to horticulture; his orchids and Malmaison roses will never be surpassed; and, having travelled much, he had a marvellous store of anecdote and scenic description wherewith to employ his confident tongue. He was an ideal host, an ideal guest. His father, a prosperous shipbuilder of humble origin, had seen with some disappointment that Nature had clearly intended Ills younger son for merely ornamental purposes; but, with the philosophy of a practical man, he had made the beat of the matter and had helped him, to,

make the most of his aptitude for drawing-room accomplishments. Dying, he had left Delling- holme, with a substantial income, to Geoffrey, and the shipbuilding business to his elder son, Bert, a beetle-browed, energetic, pushful young man who, are his fortieth year, had become the leading ship- builder of the north, and a famous matador of finance. Lucky, plucky, determined and ambitious, Bert Delling was the idol of the working-man, as his brother was the idol of society, and had been literally thrust into Parliament by an admiring populace and subsequently knighted. The brothers were the poles apart. The life of the one was work, work, work, with little thought of pleasure—of the other, pleasure, pleasure, pleasure, with never a thought of work. Even in his music, Geoffrey Delling was dreamy, sleepy, languid. He paused now in his twilight melodies with his fingers on the keys, and for some moments sat lost in thought. Then, with a sudden feeling of triumphant confidence in his fortunes, he dashed abruptly into one of his rare bravuras. So magnificent, so brilliant was the music that he did not hear the crunch of the long-expected wheels on the snow, did not hear the melodious, happy voice of his daughter, as she got out of the carriage with her maid, did not hear her hail the log-fires in the hall with a glad compliment: "You dear, delightful, dancing flames! It's been a delicious fortnight—never a happier, but no fires are like our own, are they, Alice? East or west, home is best. Take my muff, please. I'm going straight in to my father. And, Alice, lay out my violet velvet. It is my father's favourite.' And so overwhelming was the brilliant noise that Linda, standing on the threshold of the drawing-room, now wrapped in darkness save for the flickering firelight, fell back in sheer alarm. "What! All in darkness, father ? " "Here at last, then I Touch the button, Linda." A flood of eledric light, rose-shaded, dispelled the darkness and revealed to the one his lovely daughter elegantly clad in crimson gown and sealskin coat, with smart fur toque lit up with crimson quills, and to the other her handsome father wearing now his usual indulgent smile. She had only come in for his kiss of welcome, and, haying received it on red, happy lips, went out at once to dress for dinner. He did not like to be kept waiting. A little later she came into the dining-room, looking exquisite in the violet velvet that ehewed up her milk-white skin with its peachy tints on cheek and chin, and her mass of wavy red-gold hair. "What a winter, father!" she exclaimed, as she seated herself. "We got snowed up at a little junction, though not so badly but that We soon were on our way again. How the poor will suffer if this lasts, with coals at their present price! I never sit down to a feast of good things "—her eyes grew grave as their gaze_ travelled over the flower-decked, glittering table—" but I almost feel ashamed. So many have barely a crust of bread, and We have—everything. Often I am checked in the very midst of enjoyment, in the very midst of thinking how good life is, by a swift remembrance of the other side of the medal." "My love," returned her father with his pleasant smile, "you are quite Egyptian in your lugubrious table sentiments. There is a very pretty skull in some corner or other of the library which perhaps you would like to have before you as you eat. Shall I send for it?" Linda blushed a little, but laughed: good- humouredly. "How you tease me, father! But, indeed, I quite deserve it for my stupidity in regaling you with such doleful talk." She could not expect him, she thought, to feel as she did for the hardships and sorrows of the poorest poor. He had never seen one of these hideous, joyless hovels. He was a man of fashion. Solicitude for the submerged tenth was left, she mused a little sadly, to women and—curates. So she dismissed her sombre thoughts and applied herself to the pleasant task of amusing her father with descriptions of the people she had met and of the pleasures she had shared. Dinner over, Mr. Delling passed his arm affec- tionately round his daughter's slender waist, and, leading her to a palm-decked alcove in the drawing-room, stood silent till she had settled herself among the silken cushions. Then he seated himself before her, and, with eyes fixed gravely upon her face, took her slim fingers in his own. "My love," he said, slowly, "I did not want to spoil your appetite—and mine—by referring to the matter earlier, but—l have bad news for you."
" Bad—news ! "

What I want to ask you is this: Do you imagine for a moment that if you spend this fortune of yours—a happy windfall, I must say—on paying debts which need not concern you in the least, there will be anything left on which to keep up Dellingholme ? "Oh, no!" she answered, a little sadly. "I have some small notion of arithmetic, father. Dellingholme, when I have paid off the mortgage, must be let, and we must take a smaller house and try to be as happy there. Or, perhaps, for its name's sake, Uncle Bert would buy Dellingholme. It would leave me a little more money."

"A little more money!" cried her -father, scorn- fully. "Do you know what you are contemplating? These debts, if you are fool enough to pay them, will swallow more than three-fourths of your fortune! You will leave us paupers, Linda!' "Come, come, dear father," she answered, gently. "Not paupers, dearest. It is not so bad as that. What should we have done if no fortunt had been left us?" _t

"Don't worry me with 'if's,' " he retortedi fiercely. "Do you think I have notauld enough of worry ? " He had flung himself into an easy-chair, and with head thrown back stared up with angry eyes at the magnificent ceiling with its Cupids and roses. Softly his daughter came towards him, and, dropping on a knee beside him, laid loving arms about his neck. "Dear father," she said, "you have not thought over this calmly and kindly. This fortune must not be misused. The fact that Lance Tempest is most wicked with his money convinces me that it is meant for nobler uses. Honestly to pay the debts we have brought on ourselves—aye, though it brought us to the workhouse !—and afterwards to try to profit by the bad scare we have had, this is the better way. We shall be at peace with our- selves, and true friends will not--" He released himself abruptly from her arms and rose.

"You talk," he said, with icy coldness, "like a most excellent copy-book, Linda, or like a senti- mental, frightened school-girl: I had hoped you were a woman of the world. When you find you have made a considerable drop in the social scale —for bankruptcies are forgotten when you get on your feet again, but poverty that lasts is not—when you find yourself refusing brilliant entertainments because you can give none yourself, when you have had brought home to you all the losses that it means, you will regret this absurd ultra-con- scientiousness of yours. I advise you, think it over. Not every day does a fortune drop from the clouds. Be a woman of sense. You are as fond of luxury and pleasure as ever I have been." With dignified scorn he strode to the door, but there the dignity vanished, and Linda Delling, standing rooted to the spot with consternation in her eyes, heard, for the first time in her life, her father slam the door. _

Gone now was the glamour of his beauty, his mellow voice, his polished geniality. She felt herself orphaned, desolate, utterly forsaken. Then out of the misty emptiness rose another face—a kind, earnest, sincere face—the face of Ambrose Power. _ _ _
"He is one of the truest men in all the world I " she said. "And he would say I have done right."

Yes, her father was right. She loved luxury and pleasure—loved glitter and gladness; loved to go yachting with a troop of friends; loved to see new scenes, wonderful landscapes, magnificent cities. So much the more could she feel for lives un- changeably sordid, bare and dull. So much more did the sights and sounds and smells of slumdom offend her pampered senses. But her heart was brave and generous, and paid no heed to their protests. From a school-room not far from the Old Town sounded a very happy noise composed of the merry tinkle of a piano, the rhythmic stamp of some scores of little feet, the bee-like hum of half-loud

voices. Softly the Rev. Ambrose Power opened the door and looked in. Yes I The Old Town had, alas its brutal men, its frowsy women still; but here, at least, was a goodly portion of its children, their faces scrubbed by half-scornful, yet not unwilling, mothers till now they shone like glass, save where the "tide-mark" parted clean face from dirty throat. Some of them with prouder parents wore gay ribbons in their hair and gaudy beads about their necks. But all of them wore fastened at their neads bright paper flowers that deft and dainty hands had fashioned. And all of them were happy. For these were living flowers—forget-me-nets, violets, buttercups, daisies, and primroses. There were garden flowers, too—roses, lilies, pansies, pinks, and gorgeous sunflowers. But wild flowers and garden flowers were quite at peace together, and, hand-in-hand, with quite wondrous grace, they danced towards each other, and swinging round with now and then a rhythmic click of heel and toss of toe, blew merry kisses each to each at pauses in their song. Ambrose Power seated himself unmarked on a bench beside the door. "It goes extremely well," he commented, pleased. "What an angel she is!" The melodies, too, were hers. Like snow-white butterflies her twinkling fingers chased each other across the keys. She had all her father's musical skill, with a more original fancy. And this panto- mime of song and dance was called "The Meeting of the Flowers." • But. now one of the Queens of the Guild caught eight of Ambrose, and, the music happening to end just then, came rapturously towards him. "How sweet of you to come and see us.. Have you been 'here long? Don't they dance well? If only they were properly washed." "I don't think it matters, does it ? " said Ambrose, smiling. "The aim so far is just to make them happy for an hour and teach them gentler games. And you have admirably succeeded." "Oh, here is Mr. Power! How dear of him! Have you been here long? Did you see them dance? Don't they—" . "Mr. Power I This is too charming of you. How do you do? Celia, here is MI. Power. Isn't it too sweet of him ? " "How do you do, Miss Flashington ? " said Ambrose, his head beginning to swim. "And why do not the queens wear flowers ? " "Oh, Mr. Bower! ,Paper flowers? It would be too absurd." But where there is a will there is a way. The Rev. Ambrose Power had freed himself in a most polite but eely fashion from the bevy of gushing beauties, and was now alone with Linda. "Are you pleased ? " she asked. "Don't you think they look happy ?" "Indeed I do. And I marvel at their skill." "Oh, they go to penny hops,' " Linda informed hitn. "And those who don't learn from those who do. They have told me quite a lot of their little secrets." "I suppose they have. You have the gift of sympathy, and children are quick to find it out. But let me offer you my warmest congratulations, Miss Delling, on the fortune which I understand you have inherited. That it will be nobly used,l know." She looked into his ardent eyes with a little smile. "Thank you, Mr. Power. You are good to me. But the fortune will be mine a few days only. Let me tell you the truth. I have been helping my father to be very extravagant, and most of my money will be swallowed up by the appalling debts we have incurred. It, is a shameful confession, but the truth. I am not a rich woman any longer, Mr. Power; indeed, almost a poor one. But you may congratulate nie all the same, for I feel that God has been most good to me in sending me this !ortune that I never dreamt I needed." But Ambrose Power stood mute. A sudden flush rose to his brow. The barrier, then, was gone! "The carriage is coining for you, I suppose, Miss Delling ? " he asked, in a hoarse voice tkliat ne scarcely knew himself. "Oh, no. My father does not like—l mean we never have the horses out in snowy weather." "I see." Ambrose smiled a little. How careful he was of the horses. And how loyally she stood by him. Her debts, indeed! "Then I may have the pleasure of seeing you home? 1 see the others are getting ready." She would be very pleased. None of the others I were going her way. The flowers had been put ! away, the children had donned their battered hats and tattered capes, the ladies their cosy furs. In a dream Ambrose heard their voices. They were gone. The caretaker had come in and was sitting on the bench Ambrose had vacated. A moment later and the lights were out, and they two were crunching along the white streets together. They were more silent than was the wont of either, and so it came to pass that it was at the very doors of Dellingholme that had onCe so awed his love, that Ambrose Power told Linda the secret he had kept so long. And at the very doors of Dellingholme he was made harms.. WINRe pretty weaning nas just taken pmce, anc the presents Sir Bertram Delling, M. P. for Cole- borough, made to his "dear niece" were not only very substantial cheque indeed, but also time deeds of Dellingholme. [Tax END.]

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

-- 1 FLOWER Snow.—The annual show of the Penketh and Sankey Cottage Garden and Cage Bird Society was held on Saturday last in a field opposite the Infants' School, Penketh. Two large rna.rqu6s had been erected one for the fruit and flowers, and the other for the cage birds. The weather, was unfortunately. of the vilest description, and though great interest Is taken loeally in the Society's work, the attendance on Saturday, was far behind other years. Great efforts had been put forth to make the show as interesting and attractive as pos- sible, but owing to the wet weather, many items had to be omitted. The Maypole dance ef the children, a feature of last year's show, was, of course abandoned, and it was announced that the dance would be gone through on the following Thursday. The weather, how- ever,was all against this on Thursday also,and the chil- dren,and their parents and friends,thereby were greatly disappointed. The show was in every way a credit to both the committee and the exhibitors, the different classes being well contested, and some good specimens of fruit and flowers being shown. Stands of plants, not for exhibition, had been arranged by the gardeners of Mrs. Garnett and Miss Bolton, and the President Mr. .T. B. Aitken. This gentleman has ever taken a lively interest in the work of the Society, awl has done much to further its interests. In the bird exhibits, the entries had fallen a little but the birds were of an excellent character. The silver challenge cup (to be won three times to be property of the holder), was secured by Mr. Israel Hampson, who has won it each time since it was first put three years ago. The Penketh Tannery Band was present, aid played selections in the large tent dering the afternoon, The judges were :—Gardens,Mr. William Boardman; flowers, Mr. G. Clarke (Statham) ; birds, Mr. William Wellings (prescot). Messrs. George Clarke and H. Bingham, secretaries, have been unremit- ting in their endeavours to' make the show a success, and it is a great pity the day was so bad.

'BURTON BURGESSES AND SUNDAY TRAMS. The question of running the electric cars in Burton- on-Trent on Sundays has created a great controversy, and eventually it was decided to take a plebiscite of the burgesses on the subject. Reply postcards were issued,: returnable at latest on Saturday. About 90 per ant. of the burgesses recorded their opinions, the result being as follows :—For Sunday running, 6,854; against, 1,992 majority for, 4,882.
