div.p: (cop.yri.wit.

"My dear, compose yourself, I beg. To agitate oneself has never yet been of the slightest use. Yes—bad news! I am in low water, Linda, in very low water, indeed. My means are exhausted, Dellingholme is mortgaged for every penny of its worth, and the fellows are dunning me right and left. They will give me no more time. There is nothing for it now, my girl, but—the Bankruptcy Court." "Father !"
In spite of his philosophical advice, she was agitated beyond measure. She had risen; her face was utterly bereft of colour; she was trembling from head.to foot. _ _

"Father Father I How has this happened ? " He shrugged his shoulders half-impatiently. "What is the use of going into details, Linda? You have no head for such things. Indeed, I have none myself, which is partly the reason, I suppose, for this—h'm—inisfortune. We have been living above our means, of course, and then, too, a couple of years ago I made some unfortunate speculations." It was not necessary to explain that the unfortu- nate speculations had been made on the roulette- table of Monte Carlo out of sheer caprice. His daughter stood motionless like a statue of despair. "And I—l have been playing the Lady Bountiful in the slums," she said, blankly, "on money that belonged to other people. I have been giving the children summer holidays in the country and Mayday Feasts, and—oh, father " her voice broke and tears welled up. "It is too cruel." "Such misfortunes happen every day," he murmured.

"Dellingolme is ours no longer," she almost whispered. "Grandfather's house And he must have been so proud of it. Father, why did you let me go to this great party—get all these expensive gowns ? " "Because, my dear child," he answered in .his smooth, mellow tones, "I wanted my daughter to have as much amusement—be as well dressed as any other. Because lam a weak father, I daresay. Perhaps, also," his voice for a moment took a harder ring, "because I hoped you would make some use of your splendid opportunities. Sir Everest Hardy's son is no --" "Don't, father,'" she broke in, clapping her hands to her ears. "He has never been a moment in my thoughts—never will be. But, oh I" she looked at him with searching curiosity, "how strong you are, father. How calmly, philosophically you can take this horrible calamity. I—l am heart- broken!"
Then suddenly Mr. Delling rose, whipped from an inner pocket a large blue envelope, and, taking from it a letter, flourished this before her. _ _ _ _

"Dry your eyes, my daughter," he said, with dramatic solemnity, choking back a sob of emotion. "It is your unfortunate father only who is poor— is bankrupt! You, my Linda, are—an heiress " "What 1" She stared at him incredulously. "I ? An heiress I Whose heiress ? "

"Read this," he said. "It came two days age, and, as I saw it was a lawyer's letter, I took the liberty of opening it. Your godmother, Mrs. Tempest., has been true to her threat, has disowned that foolish nephew of hers for his insane marriage, and has made you, my dear, the heiress to a very pretty fortune." She took the letter and slowly read it through. Yes, it was here in black and white. She was an heiress I Her father's eyes, fixed searchingly upon her face, saw the colour return. He heldfout his arms.
"Come, my love," he said with a coaxing smile, "and let your poor father have a kiss from his lucky daughter." Somewhat coldly she suffered herself to be embraced, then freed herself.

"Why have you frightened me so, father?" she asked, indignantly. "What was your reason? How could you do it? What fear is there now of the Bankruptcy Court? Dellingholme will be ours again, and every debt be paid." "Nonsense, child!" he answered, testily. "My affairs must take their course. With my debts you have nothing at all to do. Certainly, you may pay off the mortgage on Dellingholme—it would be a very sensible investment—but as for the other matters—nonsense! There is no law--"
"Law? I have never thought of law. The law of right is enough for me. Do you mean that, having actually the tronev with which to my them. we are to—to cheat these people who have trusted us ? "
He halted in his fretful pacing, and his fine eyes were aflame.

div.head: EVENTS THE WEEK
div.p: EVENTS THE WEEK
THE GREAT RACE.

The America Cup contest is attracting prac- tically all public attention this week, and the good wishes of every Briton are with Sir Thomas Lipton. Half a century ago at the first time of asking the Americans annexed this important international trophy, and de- spite repeated attempts front all quarters and a succession of ,most exciting encounters they have managed to keep it ever since. This very fact has of late years aroused the keenest in-

terest and the utmost compe- tition on tnis side of the At- lantic, and never has this been greater than during Sir Thomas Lipton's plucky attempts Failing in 1899 with the Sham- rock, two years ago he tried againwithSham- rock H., a yacht of a different type, which was probably inferi- or to its •prede- cess r. This year for the third time he THE AMERICA CUP. has challenged, building a third Shamrock, .which is said to combine the best points of his two previous boats, and she has certainly, de- Spite Sir Thomas's usual bad luck in the way of accidents, done very well in her trials. Ex- -peas declare that she is a very fast boat in light winds, such as have been the feature of the last two races, and it was with this pur- pose in view that Messrs. Watson and Fyfe designed her. Shamrock 111. has been well tuned up off Sandy Hook; and last week she was dry-docked, scraped, and cleaned. As a final touch, Mr. Fvfe added three feet to her bowsprit to enable -her to carry extra canvas. The American defender the V.eliance, is said to be better in a strong, wind ; so it loos as iluugh the vagaries of ti.e weather may again Play a ,prominent part in the contest. The betting is very much in favour of the Yankee yacht, but Sir Thomas Lipton expresses the utmost confidence in Shamrock HI. The races, the best out of five, take place oyer.a triangular course, and there is a time limit, which has in previous years played a promi- nent part, so that the 'series is .-often pro- longed. The races are sailed at intervals of aday- It is to be hOped that Sir Thomas Lipton,, who has proved himself a good sports- man, will have better luck this year, and be successful in "liftim;" the Cup: His victory would be highly popular all over the country.

div.head: PROPOSED CATHEDRAL FOR LIVERPOOL.
div.p: THE PROPOSED CATHEDRAL FOR LIVERPOOL.

As a result of the competition for the design for a proposed cathedral at Liverpool, five sets of drawings were sent in and judged by the advisory architects to the executive of the cathedral 'committee; The judges, who were Messrs. G. F. Bodley, R.A., and R. Norman Shaw; R.A., pronounced in favour of the design submitted by Mr. G. Gillant Scott, who is a grandson of the distinguished leader of the school of Gothic revivalists, Sir G. Gilbert Scott, R.A. The cathedral building com- mittee, not considering that the design fully :met the requirements of the case in securing :ample room ior the accomodation of a large congregation within sight and hearing of the
FINISHED

preacher, appointed Mr. Body,R.A., and Mr. G. Gilbert Scott, joint architects, thus securing the experience of the greatest modern ex- ponent of Gothic architecture and the brilliant talent of Mr. Scott, and they have now instructed their architects to prepare the plans for the new cathedral with such modifications as they might think desirable. It is hoped that the foundation stone may be laid next spring. The principle dimensions of the cathe- dral, taken from Mr. Scott's drawings, are as follows: Total length over all, 530 ft. ; total length of nave, 224 ft. ; total width of nave between the piers, 50ft. ; total length across transepts, 198 ft. ; total height of nave vault- ing, 116 ft. ; total width of north facade, 196 ft. ; .total height of towers, 2601 t.

div.head: AN UNLUCKY OFFICIAL.
div.p: AN UNLUCKY OFFICIAL.

an China they have a rough and ready way of dealing with unsuccessful offitials. It is inclined to remind one of Voltaire's well- known saving that in England they hang admirals once a month "four encourager les autres." This is certainly a libel on England, esipecially of late years, when re- tirement is the worst that ever falls to the lot of an unsuccess- ful soldier or sailor: but it is in the main principle correct about China. In China: it is cer- tainly better to be a humble nobody than a high official, as the fall is in pro- portion to the eminence, and usually comes THE /LL-FATED MARSHAL sooner or later. The most recent sou. instance is that
of Marshal Sou,

whose portrait vWe give. He was sent off with a flourish of trumpets to crush the rebellion in the province Of Konang-Si, but his efforts did not meet with very marked success. " He was, therefore, summoned - back to Pekin and received in audience by that masterful lady, the Dowager Empress, -who put him through his facings. Subsequently he was several times ordered to aPpegar before her councillors in session, who ProseTuted a vigorous cross-examination, but -apparently with unsatistactery results. The latest rumour in the Chinese capital is that during the course of the aptumn this unfortu- nate soldier, the well-known Marshal Sou, will be called upon to face the executioner— doubtless "to encourage others" to do their best. Meanwhile the rebellion in the province Of Konang-Si continues to flourish and .perturb :the authorities at headquarters.

div.head: SPANS THE FAMOUS LOCH ETIVE.
div.p: SPANS THE FAMOUS LOCH ETIVE.

The railway viaduct across Loch Etive on 'the new extension of the sellander and Oban Railway between Connel Ferry and Balla- chulish, which was opened last week, crosses the narrowest part of the loch at the Falls of Lora, which at spring tides have a drop of 4 feet in a length of about 400 yards. The 'current both on the tlood and on the ebb is

div.head: NEW VIADUCT.
div.p: THE NEW VIADUCT.

way of 5o feet between high water and the under -side of the bridge. From high water to the highest point of the bridge is 123 feet. The bridge is on the cantilever system, with an independent middle span of 232 feet rest- ing upon the ends of the cantilevers. The weight of the steel-work in the bridge amounts altogether to a little over 2, coo tons. The contractors are Arrol's Bridge and Roof Com- pany of Glasgow, and they are to be con- gratulated on the accurate manner in which the work has come together. Loch Etive is an ancient submerged glen. The scenery round it is exceptionally beautiful, and readers of Scott and Stevenson know the romantic associations of the place which has now been brought so easily within the tourist's reach.

div.head: POST OFFICE'S NEW SECRETARY.
div.p: POST OFFICE'S NEW SECRETARY.

Recently there have been various alterations in the Treasury appointments; and amongst those who have come in for promotion is Mr, Henry Babington Smith, who has been made secretary of the General Post Office. He has had a most distinguished career, especially in appointments of a "financial nature: and his

selection to this ~...-.4.....-. important post at the G.P.O. , _ . has given . ..,, . , general satisfac- tion. Probably .; he is the best man who could .., have been chosen—a thing which cannot A - - , - al ways be said A of public ap- ...r, : • I, : . A iL if ; . r pointments! 'rhe son of Mr. Archibald Smith, F.R.S.,
of jordanhill, Renfr ew-shire __ _ ,
Mr. Henry MR. HENRY BABINGTON SMITH. Babington
Smith was born

in 1863 and was educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge. At the University he had a brilliant career, taking a double first in classics, and being awarded the Chancellor's Medal. His first public appointment was that ef an examiner in the Education Department at the age of twenty-four. Four years later he commenced his connection with matters finan- cial by • being appointed principal private Eecretary to Mr. (now Lord) Goschen, who was •then Chancellor of the Exchequer. In 1892, a year later, he became a clerk in the Treasury, and was appointed secretary to the British delegates at the Brussels Monetary Conference. From 1894 to 1899 Mr. Babington Smith was private secretary to the Earl of Elgin during his term of office as Viceroy of India, for which he was decorated with the C.S.I. One of the particularly happy results of this ap- pointment was his marriage in 1898 to the Lady Elizabeth Bruce, the daughter of Lord Elgin. Upon his return to England in 1899 he was despatched upon a financial mission to the Government of Natal; and so successful was he that in the following year he was made British Representative on the Council of Administration of the Ottoman Public Debt, becoming President of -that Council a year later. For his services he was rewarded with a C. 8.; and now, to add to his unbroken record of success, has come the important appointment chronicled above.

div.head: WOEFUL JAMAICA.
div.p: WOEFUL JAMAICA.

Jamaica, the island which has just been devastated by a cyclone, has been a strange mixture of prosperity and distressfulness. Port Royal, one of the shief towns, was destroyed by an earthquake in 1692, and in 1865 the negroes rose against the whites, and massacred wholesale. Round the coast are several large and, before the cyclone, flourishing towns. Kingston, the capital, which is reported to have suffered severely, is a handsome seaport in the south-east of the island. It boasts of an up-to-date electric tramway, and its omnibus and cab fares are on a large and magnificent scale. Port Antonio, which is a jewel of the tropics, was right in the terrific heart of the cyclone. It looks out on to a bay whose waters are a clear deep blue, its white houses are shaded by mighty trees, and it is backed by high ground, which is covered with trees and plants, and looks like a wall of solid olive
PORT ANTONIO, WHICH HAS BEEN PRACTICALLY
WIPED OUT BY THE CYCLONE

green. Port Antonio is American in everything except being in 4merican territory. It is practically run by an American corporation, the United Fruit Company, whose fleet fill the berths at the wharves, and whose employees are most of the population. The flourishing little port seems to have been practically wiped off the map. At present Jamaica is making a reputation as a producer of bananas in rivalry to the Canary Islands, and as a winter resort. The American authoress, Ella Wheeler Wilcox, has written fluently in its praise in the latter respect. "What are you thinking about, you northern men and women, who rush to Florida or Bermuda, or Europe in search of. a winter resort, where comfort apd pleasure, can be found? Why do you not know of thiE lost Garden of Eden—this incomparable combination Of American comfort, English cleanliness, and Italian climate? And such beauty, such glory of colouring, such opulence of nature's best guts!" And—which is not always the case in tropical Gardens of Eden— nature has not balanced matters by being equally opulent with her worst gifts. "I have not felt one mosquito, so far," says Miss Wilcox, in mingled surprise and gratitude, "and have seen but two flies. There are no reptiles, and there is fruit and there are vegetables enough to keep one well and hearty y.t small cost and with small labour.'i

SOM E of Mr THE VEILED PROPHET CHA MBE It L A I N' S OF "FISCAL POLICY." supporters are

singularly indiscreet" There is, for example, the case of Mr. GRIFFITH. BOSCAWEN, M.P. This gentleman has been writ- ing to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN on behalf of the Tariff Reform League with the object of getting some- thing direct and definite concerning the Colonial Secretary's proposals. It might reasonably have been supposed that the members of the Tariff Reform League, Mr. GRIFFITH BOSCAWEN included, would have ascertained what is direct and definite in Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S proposals before forming themselves into an organisation to support them. To found a Church and then to make inquiry for the doctrine that is to be ' taught in it, is hardly a reasonable proceeding. " My committee," writes Mr. BOSCAWEN, " feel that in face of the misrepresentations which have been so freely made a short and definite statement from you might be of the greatest value at the present moment." Doubtless it would; but Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is not in the mood to make definite statements. His reply is certainly short, but is of a kind to make confusion worse confounded. He says that he has not suggested any tax on raw materials" such as wool or cotton." To have been definite, he should have left out the words we have placed between quotation marks. The question concerning the taxation of food is really not answered at all. "As regards food," the Colonial SECRETARY says," there is nothing in the policy of tariff reform which I have put before the country which nee.l increase in the slightest degree the cost of living of any family In this country." It was hardly worth the trouble of writing a letter if it was only to elicit such a cryptic reply as this. Unfortunately, too, for Mr. GRIFFITH BOSCAWEN, the letter is one in which he gives himself away. He has evidently failed to make himself so fully acquainted as he ought to be with the utterances of his veiled prophet. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN perceives this, and takes advan- tage of the circumstances. Instead of referring him to definite statements previously made,he puts his correspondent off by saying that there is nothing in his scheme which need increase the cost of living. This is merely an opinion which is opposed to all experience and common sense, and, beyond this, an opinion in which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN can hardly himself be a believer,since not very long ago be told the House of Commons how he is prepared to go into the workman's house and say: "Now this policy, if it is carried out, will cost you so much a week more than you pay at present for your food . . . and I will give you a table from which you can tell for yourself how much extra wages you must get in order to cover the extra expense of living. There is no want of definiteness here. An increase of the cost of food was so much a part of the plan that it had to be balanced by a promise of increased wages. It is not convenient for Mr. GRIFFITH BOSCAWEN and his Tariff Reform League to put things in that frank way; but does he not think there is a certain impudence in describing as misrepresentations what are accurate renderings of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S woras ? We must really ask these Tariff Reform geotlemen to be a little more straightforward with the public. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has not advocated the taxation of raw material; but nobody ever accused him of doing so. It has merely been pointed out that a scheme of preference for the Colonies is impossible without the taxa- tion of raw materials. Canada sends us corn, timber, and pulp made from timber. How is a preference to be established unless corn from the United States, and timber from the Baltic, and pulp from Sweden, are to be taxed ? Australia sends us great quantities of wool. It is not possible to give any beneficial preference to Australia without putting a tax on foreign wool. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN may, and evidently does, Con- sider it discreet not to speak of the taxation of raw materials; but any system of preferential tariffs for the benefit of the Colonies necessarily involves such a form of taxation. The letter sent to Mr. GRIFFITH BOSCAWEN is significant of the concealments which it is necessary to practise lin order to commend Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S policy to public favour. The policy will not bear the ordeal of definite statement. It is a policy of "open your mouth and shut your eyes," and it is based for the most part on an undiscerning con- viction that the British public is about as simpl e as a crowd in a country fair. We are of opinion nevertheless, that before the" big figln " has gone much further the people will be found insisting on. some more precise information as to what it is all about. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN will be required to give to the public what he has refused in a roundabout way to Mr. GRIFFITH BOSCAWEN, who really should be more careful about attributing mis- representation to those who merely do not agree with him, and who have the best reasons possible for not agreeing with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN.

WHATEVER the final ' THE RACE FOR result of the present THE CUP. series of races, the American Cup will, no doubt, continue to be the subject of friendly contention between ourselves and the United States for the length of many lifetimes. Whether the Cup is on one side of the Atlantic or the other there will be men who, at whatever cost, are determined to lift it. Never was there a case so stirringly illustrative of the old Greek saying, "The reward is in the race we win, and not in the

prize." The prize in this instance is only of small intrinsic value. It is worth 100 or so. The stakes in a second or third-rate horse race are usually worth that amount several times over; and yet it costs £60,000 or £70,000 to build a yacht capable of crossing the Atlantic with a view to the winning of the cup. There is nothing that thisl country has desired more to recover, or that Americans have been more determined to keep. When the R)yal Yacht Squadron offered this trophy for competition nobody ever dreamt of America as a competitor, and still less that the Cup would be won by United States yachtsmen, and held by them against all competitors for fifty two years. The victory of a little schooner called the America was one of the greatest surprises in the history of sport. The America belonged to the New York Yacht Club; but in England there was no apprehension as to what the New York yachtsmen could do, and astonishment was there- fore unbounded when the rakish-looking American craft. "a low, black hull, two noble sticks of ex- traordinary rake," outsailed fifteen British yachts and came in an easy winner.

Englishmen love pluck, and daring, and success. The astonishing loss of the Cup was, of course, a matter for deep disappointment; but the manner in which the trophy was won gained the admiration of lovers of sport of all kinds and degrees. The late UEEN, PRINCE CONSORT, and the present KING, then a very small Prince of Wales, had watched the race and witnessed the victory, and one of the QUEEN'S first acts was to summon Commodore JEVONS, the skipper of the America, to receive her congratulations. The Commodore was, indeed, made almost as much of on this side of the Atlantic as if he were an Englishman who had been to the other side to snatch an American trolihy. When the Royal Yacht , Squadron offered its cup as the prize in a competi- tion "open to yachts belonging to the clubs of all nations,"its members did not believe that America could build yachts fit to compete with those which were built for English waters. It was not yet known that the United States had mastered the art of building the finest and fleetest vessels in the world. But now that a lesson had been learnt no time was lost before the commencement of efforts to profit by it. The idea that nobody could build yachts like our own was abandoned at once, the contrary having been so distinctly proved. Yachts were built on American principles, with stich improvements as our own buildsrs designed, and with such consequences that we easily held our own in successive inter- national contests. But the Cup had gone to the United States, and American possession of it was never challenged until 1870, when, Mr. JAMES ASHBURY'S yacht having beaten that of Mr. GORDON BENNETT across the Atlantic, the owner incontinently challenged the Cup-owners, with the result that he got handsomely beaten, his yacht corning in as the seventh in the race.

There was a time Alen Lord DUNRIVEN seemed certain to bring the Cup home again. This was in 1895. DITNRAVEN yacht, VALKYRIE 111., won the secolid race, but it had accidentally struck Defender at the outset; and though it was per- mitted to start, and to finish the race, it was afterwards disqualified for the foul. And then it was seen that a yacht race may be no less prolific in the breeding of international disagreements than in the promotion of international amity. Grave, indeed,were the incidents to which this unfortunate race gave rise, but they have been happily obscured by the genial personality of Sir THOMAS LIPTON, who struck the American imagination from the first, and speedily obtained on the other side of the Atlantic such a popularity as hardly any other person born on this side of "the herring- pond" has ever possessed. Sport, as Sir THOMAS LIPTON has pursued it, has proved to be a great reconciler, and the later contests for the American Cup have done more to cement friendship between this country and the United States than all our trade on the one hand, and all our diplomacy on the other.

Mr. R. A. Naylor is feeling " the fascination of a glorious uncertainty" at Carnarvon,and whether he wins or loses hopes to remain "as happy and contented as heretofore." We should have thought his state of happiness " heretofore " was not altogether enviable seeing that he has for so long been driven from house and home by the Thel- wall nuisance. However, in this matter at least, he doubtless knows best. In another column we publish a letter from him further ex- plaining his position with the Non-Traders, and giving the reasons for his recent very candidly expressed opinion that if he stood, he would most certainly be elected for Warrington. Apparently Mr. Naylor's confidence is based on his belief that the Non-Traders can do anything in Warrington— whichiis open to doubt.Mun'cipal trading:might not prove so potent in Parliamentary as In municipal matters. Perhaps it was the lack in Warrington of " the fascination of a glorious uncertainty" which caused Mr. Naylor to forsake us for Carnar- von Boroughs. He has our best wishes.

Warrington is surrounded by a rich agricultural diAriat and it is not surprising to find that a keen interest is taken in the study of horticulture. Evidence of this has been afforded during the past few days, for no fewer than three flower shows have been held in the immediate district. On Satur- day, there were exhibitions at Stockton Heath and Penketh, and again on Trinrsdav the annuil fliwer show at Hatton took place. The Stockton Heath Garden Society promoted the show at Stockton Heath, and although a very young institution, it gives promise of a useful and successful future. Reference was made to the marked improvement which was noticeable in the village in the cultivation of plants, flowers and vegetables, due to the healthy rivalry which the G rclen Swiety encourages. The President put in a strong claim for the Society b- cause it tended to encourage the working c!Psses to take a pride in their gardens and to brighten their homes. In this opinion he has a strong supporter in Dean Hole, Who as a cultivator of roses, has gained a high reputation. ' Writing to the promoters of a meeting held at Heywood to consider the proposal to form a horti- cultural society for Heywood and district the Dean wrote: "If you can induce a working Man to take some pains with his vegetables, and teach his wife how to cook them, you will do more to keep him sober than all the blue ribbon and pledges worn or signed.' After such strong commenda- tion, local horticultural societies ought not to lack support or encouragement from all who are inter- ested in the welfare of the community.

The double drowning fatality at Latchford ought certainly to awaken the authorities to the necessity for some precautionary measures. This 1 particular swing-bridge, near the railway embank- ment, has for years been a play-thing and a death- trap combined for the children of the neighbour- hood. Boys will be boys,and no amount of warn- ing will deter them from a dangerous amusement. In this case the fun consists in swinging the bridge—which is actuated by the old-fashioned pole—and seeing how wide a gap between the end of the:structure'and the embankment can be jumped with safety. The exactdistance is only ascertained by the sudden immersion of an over-venturesome jumper. We understand something of the sort occurred on Wednesday evening, when two unfor- tunate boys were drowned, one in trying to rescue

the other. What is required is a locking arrange- ment which will prevent the bridge becoming the dangerous plaything of small boys, and the neglect to provide some such safeguard appears to us almost criminal. If the starting mechanism of one of the great Ship Canal swing bridges was left the mercy of passers-by there would be an immedi- ate and loud outcry. The only difference baween the two analogies is in the size of the bridges.

Apart from the dangerous character of this bridge, the fatality brings into prominence the heroism of the boy Wilson. Although only tee years of age he succeeded on the first of this month in rescuing a boy from drowninr, in a clay pit. Oil Wednesday evenit.g he risked ''his life a secoo" time in the hope of rescuing a young playmate °f his named Corbett,who had fallen into the C n This time he was unsuccessful and Ps' the penalty with his lite. Such actionss as these stamp young Wilson as , little hero, and it issa.tisfactory to learn that his bravo deeds have not passed unnoticed. On t,h: day of his death, inquiries were being made by the Royal Humane Society with reference to /us former exploit, and another recognition of it was to have been made at the school he attended IV the presentation of a silver medal. He has neib, , lived bo be so honoured, but his brave actions 04° ' not be lost on his school-fellows. The Coroner ,1 who conducted the inquiry yesterday expressed the sentiments of the jury when he said that he would have been proud to be the father of suet' :fin lad, who having saved one life lost his own attempting to save another,

A GOOD REsottrrroN.—Wear ALE' TAYLOR's Wonderful Boots.—Advt. Another Warrington Fire. The premises occupied by' Mr. William Beswick, hardware. and smallware dealer, Battermarket-street, Were early on Saturday meriting the scene of a fire Which, but for the valuable services rendered by the 'fire brigade.,might have had very serious results. The alarm was given at 4 15 by Constable Barton, and the 'firemen quickly• turned out under the commend of _Superintendent and Deputy Superintendent Turner. iFt was found that the warehouse and stable at the rear of the shop were well ablaze and the efforts of the brigade weie at once put forth tf.° prevent the flames from spreading to the front .block of property. In this the men were success- -111, although they had a difficult task. A pony which was in the stable was unfortunately roasted to death. Spector Taylor and a number ormen endeavoured _o release it soon after the outbreak was discovered, but were unable to force the stable door open. A trap was also destroyed. The warehouse was almost gutted and the contents were rendered useless. Some Paraffin oil was stored on the premises but the firemen succeeded in saving it from the flames. After about two hours' work the fire was got under control, but in the meantime the roof of the warehouse had fallen in. Damage to the extent of several hundred pounds was done but it is covered by insur- ance. How the fire originated is not known, but it is thought that rats nibbling at some matches niight have caused the outbreak. LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER the CLOCK. BRrD OE-STREET.—Ad. 'Death of Mr. John Westgarth, sen. Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mr. John Westgarth, who passed away at the resid- taco of his daughter, Mrs. James Kershaw, Knutsford- road, Latchford, on Wednesday, at the ripe old age of 'PI. The deceased gentleman. who was well-known la Warrington, had only been ill two or three days, 'and to within a few hours of his death retained full Possession of his faculties. He was • born fit Gamblesbv in Cumberland in 1812 and lived there until 1839 when he removed to Liverpool. He was engaged in a fruit warehouse in that city for about five years and in 181.1 came •to Warrington. From that Year untillB73 he was employed in this town by the London and North Western Railway Company, and for the greater part of that time filled the responsible -position of Chief inspector on the platforms first at the old Bank Quay Station and afterwards at the exist- ing station. After 28 years' faithful service at War- rington he was promoted to the position of station master at Walton-Ali-Hill, near Liverpool, anti remained there until 1886, thus completing 41 years -unbroken service in the Company's employ. On his retirement, which was brought about tot by physical incapacity but through failing sight he returned to Warrington and lived with his daughter, Mrs. Kershaw -until his death. He leaves two children—Mr. John Westgarth, of Sheffield, and Mrs. Kershaw, Warring- ton. The funeral will take place at the Cemetery to- -morrow (Sunday). • FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street,Warringion.—Advt. - Gas Workers' and General Labourers' Union. An open air meeting under the auspices of the above Union was held on the vacant land offForster-street,on Monday evening. The chair was taken by Mr. F. Stott (secretary Warrington Trades and Labour Couu- -61). In his remarks he said that never was there a Period in the history of the Trades Unions movement When it was more necessary that men should combine. The cost of living had during the past few years greatly increased, but the wages of the labourers of Warrington still remained the same. It was wrong Perhaps to call the sum of 17 or 18 shillings per week Wages, but that was the amount which thousands of labouring men were receiving in return for a week's work. He asked them to point out to him 3n37 way in which these wages could be 11,1 creased exciSpt by the Trade Union Organiza- en—gr. ClYnes, the district secretary for ~,aricashire, then addressed the meeting. His agthess was exceedingly pointed and practical. He re numerous instances shewing how the. organisa- tion had been beneficial in securing increased wages a.nd reduction of hours, and in many cases preventing a r veduction of . wages. Their ,organisation was the gest Labourers Union in existence, having over .I.°o branches. It was affiliated to the General Federa- tion of Trades Unions. div.head: " Countess's " Unpaid Fine.
div.p: The " Countess's " Unpaid Fine.

•An application was 'ma-de to the magistrates at Stockport on Wednesday with reference to Agnes Gilroy, of Congleton, who has represented herself to be the aiountess of Stamford and Warrington. Some time ago she was fined for travelling on the London and North-Western Railway Company's system with- out paying her fare. Detective Parsons stated that the fine was not paid, and a distress warrant was issued and a diligent search made, but no goods were found to distrait" upon. The magistrates ordered the defendant, who did not appear, to be committed to prison for °Tie month.

div.head: BEST BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER the CLOCK.—.A.dvt.
div.p: BEST BOOTS FOR ALL.—UNDER the CLOCK.—.A.dvt.

Sunday School Teachers' Trip. I The teachers of St. Paul's and All Saints' Sunday schools had their annual outing on Monday, and a very enjoyable affair it was. Accompanied by the Rev. T. W. Barber, Mrs. Barber,' and Miss Westwell; the party, numbering about 20, journeyed to Llan- gollen by the 8.15 a.m. train. On arrival breakfast was served, and afterwards the teachers dispersed in groups to enjoy themselves according to inclination. The manyplaces of interest in the beautiful vale were visited, the country being at it& best. During the day the party was joined by the Vicar and Mrs. Brace- camp, who had journeyed from Llanfairfech.an. After the substantial meal, provided by Mr. Faulkner, of the Hand Hotel, the %Vicar referred to his military adventures while acting as chaplain to the Volunteers in the Isle of Man, and cordially thanked those who took so deep an interest in the Sunday school work. The return was accomplished in safety, after an eminently successful: excursion.
UNDER the CLOCK or GOOD BOOTS.—Advt. Serious Cycle Accident. _

On Monday evening a shocking cycle accident occurred at Three Road Ends, Higher Walton. Thomas Tarran, lay reader, Preston Brook-, was. cycling home, and turning the corner at Higher Walton he encountered two traps, belonging respec- tively to Mr. Wood, greengrocer, Tanner's-lane, War- rington, and Mr. Cliffe, Warrington. In. trying to pass he ran into Mr. Wood's horse, which fell upon him and his bicycle. Mr. Cliffe jumped, from his trap and quickly raised the fallen horse. - The bicycle was twisted into scrap metal, and Tarran was seriously injured. His knees were terribly cut, and just above the right knee was a hole an inch and a half wide :penetrating to the bone. Constable Miller rendered first aid, and sent Tarran home in a trap, Dr. Bower being summoned. Mr. Wood's horse was badly in- jured, but Mr. Wood was unhurt. While Mr. Cliffe was rendering assistances his young horse galloped off and reached Norton Priory, Runcorn, before being stopped. Walking Contest. _ _ _ _ _

A. walling contest organized by the employs of Messrs. S. Reynolds and Company, tanners, Latch- ford, took place on Saturday afternoon. The course was front Latchford to Hoo Green and back, a distance of nearly fourteen Miles. Despite the unfavourable weather thirteen competitors turned out, and a very g)ocl pace was maintained.—The following were the winners :—•
SCRATCH RACE.
Hrs. Min. Sec. 1 A. Jenks 2 W. Dakin 3 A. Fenton 2 ... 31 ... 40

HANDICAP RACE. 1 A. Jenks - lmin. 2 F. Selby 3 A. Fenton 4 „ > IP 4 W Dakin • ~ ~Scratch. The prizes were provided by the generosity of Mr. John Coon and Mr. John Reynolds. The following gentlemen acted as checkers on the route : —Mr. J. Boscow, Mr. M. Lomas, Mr. T. H. Houghton, Mr. A. Hale. Mr. A. Grounds was starter, and Mr. F. Short judge.

Bold-street Wesley Guild. A very successful outing in connection with this guild took place last week when, at the kind in- vitation of Mr. and Mrs. T. B. Carter, the members paid a visit to Eversley, Frodsham. The party,which numbered over 50, included the circuit ministers,Revs. G. H. Carson, R. Wilkins Rees and W.C. J. Neville, and left Bank Quay Station by the 2.20 train. On arriving at the house, the visitors Wire received by Mr, and Mrs. Carter. Games of all kinds had been. pro- vided, including billiards, ping-pong (on the lawn), croquet, bowls, and quoits, and when tired of these there were the greenhouses and gardens to be explored, the beauties of which must be seen to be appreciated. Tea was served on the lawn, and all the members did full justice to the bountiful supply of good things- placed before them. The Rev. G. H. Carnson, on behalf of the Guild,tha,nked Mr. and Mrs. Carter, for their kindness, and in replying Mr. Carter expressed the hope that a similar visit might be paid next year. Photographs of the party were taken, and the rest of the evening spent in games of various kinds. Good-byes were said about eight o'clock, and on the way to .the statinn all expressed the opinion that the outing had been one of the best the Guild had ever had.

Lifeboat Saturday Demonstration. • I. The arrangements ;or the demonstration on Saturday September sth. are being rapidly 'pushed forward. and , another largely - attended meeting of the general committee was held at tire Town Hall last evening under the presidency of Mr. D. Davies. —The Chairman, • announced that during the , ensuing week a:special appeal would be made for funds ! with which to obtain prizes.Abont £l5 or :£2O would be amply sufficient. Councillorlienry Thornton has already promised assistance.—The Hon. Secretary (Mr. Stanley Wilson) said Mr. W. Parkinson had offered to give an aquatic .firework display on the evening of the 'demonstration.—The Committee tender .ed their thanks to Mr. Parkinson for his. offer, but regretted that they • could not accept it owing to the risks and difficulties which would be entailed. —c.iieuncillor J. Roberts reported that the services of 400 collectors had been obtained and it was proposed 'to allot dis- tricts to certain numbers —The Chairman reported that the old bank premises at Market Gate had been placed at the disposal of the committee by the Finance Committee and would be. used for committee meetings, advertising purposes, &.:c —The Hon. Secretary said that " boat " collecting - boxes would be sent out to local hotels to-dak (Satur-- day).,—Mr. E. A. Sanders announced several attractive , features of the procession. il

The Police Sports. The wretched weather on Thursday made it ina. pos- sible to hold the annual sports organized by the Police Athletic Club and the officials took the only reasonable course in deciding upon a postponement. Conse- quently the sports will take place on Thursday next, and in view of the rather Serious loss entailed by the postponement it is to be hoped that the generous patronage of the public will be forthcoming. There were no fewer than 230 entries for Thursday's meet- ing, and of these 117 competitors were .from distant and adjacent towns. Some of the competitors were communicated with by, telegraph and telephone and booking clerks at certain stations were informed of the postponement in order that they might impart the news to competitors who applied for tickets for Warrington. T'is an ill wind that blows nobody good, and =tiny newsboys and other Poor children at any rate had cause to be thankful. at the unexpected turn of events. Nearly 400 sandwiches had been pur- chased for competitors and others, and it was decided to distribute them to deserving children. All the afternoon the Police • Station was literally beseiged with hungry youngsters and it goes without saying that there was no -difficulty in disposing of the sand- wiches. It is unfortunate that the athletic club has no reserve fund to meet the loss incurred, all the profits in former years having been given to local charities. This year, it is hoped to swell the ftrilds of the Infir- mary, District Nursing Association, and Police Athletic Club, and given fine weather there should be a large attendance at Wilderspool on Thursday after- noon.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday August 22, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday August 22, 1903.

Lord Justice Sir John RigbY, of Carlyle House, Chelsea Embankment, a native of Runcorn, £705,588. William Pilkington, of Roby Hall, Liverpool, and of Messrs. Pilkington Bros., Limited, St. Helens, colliery owners and glass manufacturers, £107,658. The Re-opening of Parr Hall. .

Parr Half is a-t- present being re-decorated by Messrs. J. Hesketh and Sons, Ltd„ and already the appearance of the building has been greatly improved. The Warrington Dramatic Society will have the honour of giving the re-opening performances in the hall on September 30th, October .Ist and 2nd, when they will present Mr. J. H. Byron's original comedy "Our boys" Some years ago this amusing piece was given by the DramaticS,Soctety and no doubt 'the forthcoming revival will be attended with success. The proceeds will be in aid of the Warrington Infirmary and other local charities.

C heshire Labourer Buried Alive. At Barnton, Northwich, on Holiday, C ironer Yates investigated the death of John lloss, sixty, labourer. Evidence showed that on Saturday the man was Cart- ing Sand from Oakwood-lane to Yew Tree Farm. Suddenly he was missed from where he had been working. A quantity of sand, estimated at nine or ten tons, had fallen, burying him alive. He was dug out quite dead. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. Cheshire Salt Shipments.

On Tuesday moriiiig the official statistics of the salt shipments from the Mersey ports were issued. They show that during July 62,395 tons were exported and coasted, representing a depression on a corresponding period of nearly 21,000 tons. Liverpool's shipments were 45,174, and Runcorn and Manchester shipments came to 17,221 tons. Almost every country reeeived less salt, the United States disclosing a reduction of 3,3:59 tons, British North America a redaction of 3,000, Africa over 2,003, Asia 10,600, and the coast- wise shipments a reduction of 5,000. Death of Mr. John Bradford.

We regret to announce the death ,of Mr. John Bradford, a gentleman well known in Cheshire farm- ing circles, who pissed away at his residence -" Reddish H mse," Whitefield-road, Stockton Heath, yesterday Morning. The dgseased gentleman' who was in his 75th year, had for Not* time suffered from art internal complaint. Up to two years ago he carried on the farm attached to " Reddish Hall," Grapp3nhall, which is one of the largest farms in the district, but on account of failing health he was obliged to retire, and • went to live at Stockton Heath. Mr. Bradford was a life trustee of Hill Cliff° Baptist Chapel, and for some years repre- sented Grappenhall on the *Runcorn Rural District Council and Board of Guardians. He retired about two years ago. He leaves four sons and one daughter. The -funeral will take place at Hill Cliffe on Monday. LORD SALISBURY.

div.head: MR. R. A. NAYLOR AND THE NONTRADERS.
div.p: MR. R. A. NAYLOR AND THE NON- TRADERS.
The " Fascination of a Glorious Uncertainty" at Carnarvon.

Mr. R. A. Naylor writes from St. Michael's House. Egerton Gardens, London, S.W. as follows : Sir,—l have been interested in the comments in your last edition re the Non-Traders and the com- ing parliamentary vacancy. lam under the impres- sion that neither political parties in your Borough appreciate fully, tha great strength of this organization. I was led to associate myself with it from the fact that some of its mem- bers were refused the very Modest request of seeing certain Corporation accounts. I then thought, like many do now, that as regards power, the Non-Traders were an insignificant quantity, and this was why I supported them i their reasonable endeavour to obtain information from the particu- lar source from which every ratepayer has a moral, if nota legal right to expect it. The expression of my sympathetic leanings was the cause of my receiv- ing and accepting an invitation to one of their meetings ; but I was never more surprised than in finding how wrongly I had calculated the strength of the Association. For solidarity and unanimity of feeling I never saw the like in Warrington, and any of your readers who doubt the power of such a deter- mined body of men,- even to elect a Parliamentary candidate of their own choice, are evidently not acquainted with the fact that no party has ever before held the destinies of a Warrington election in its hands with such certainty. Had I acquiesced in the kind suggestion of these gentlemen to accept the candidature; not only on their word of honour, but upon the evidences of my own observations, I should have done so, believing that defeat was quite impossible. However I have declined this and other appar- ently safe 'seats and have now definitely accepted the unanimous invitation of the Fair-Traders of the Caruarvon Boroughs, and this mainly through the difficulties surrounding such a contest. So far I have had a magnificent reception but as the result has at present the fascination of a glorious uncertainty I will not prophesy, but whether I win or losel hope I shall remain as happy and conten- ted as heretofore. I think the people of Warrington of all shades of political thought who have been good enough to wish me success, and whether the Non-Traders of your town bring out a. special candidate or whether the electors are appealed to through the ordinary channels of party, the contest will be watched with great interest by your Obedient servant, R. A. NAYLOR. August 18th, 1903.

div.head: HIS CANDIDATURE. The Fiscal Question.
div.p: HIS CANDIDATURE. The Fiscal Question.

Mr. Naylor, the Conservative candidate for the Car- narvon boroughs, on Thursday night attended a" most enthusiastic " meeting of members of the Bangor Con- servative Club and others in the club, and was accorded an extremely cordial reception. Col. Marshall, ,president of the club, occupied the chair, and said that he had the greatest pleasure in in- troducing a man who had come forward in a most patrio- tic and public-spirited manner. as a candidate in the Unionist interest at the next election (cheers.) Mr. Naylor had had offers to contest other constituencies, which perhaps would be easier to fight than the one he was now determined to stand for, but from what he had seen of him he was possessed of a fighting spirit. (Loud cheers). Mr. Naylor said he OA not come there as a party man in the strict sense of. the word, but as a "true lover of his native land." (Cheers.) He supported the Union- ist party because they recognised the principles end opinions which he held dear, and which he would not part with even to catch votes. (Cheers.) He would not wait for the Government to say what he mast do. H 8 had his programme ready, and by that programme he was prepared to stand or fall. (Cheers). With regard to the fiscal question he found that people were already grumbling about it. They wereanswering Mr. Chamber- lain before he had any chance of making his statement. If not very much deceived in Mr. Chamberlain, he felt quite sure he would give the country an eye-opener when he fully explained his views, America was the strongest protective country in the world, and yet the wages paid there were the highest. She exported twice as much as she imported, and most of the money resulting therefrom came from the pockOts of Britishers. The contrary was the case in the United Kingdom, which negatived the prevailing theory when Free Trade was originated that the exports would be paid for by the imports. Within the (last 18 years the ex- portation of manufactured goods for this country had only increased by 31 per cent.. while for Germany during the mime period it had increased by 35i per cent., and for America it .had increased 174 per cent. He wondered whether a little protection in this country would not produce sonnl increase in the exports. (Cheers). It might be asked what this country should do if foreign nations did not supply us with food and other goods. Let them look to Canada the granary of the world. Had we only done our duty to Canada in the past we should not new be importing £60,000,000 worth from America and only .C 16,000,000 worth from our own 'dependencies. His impress ion was that Mr. Chamberlain had come to the rescue of our trade in the nick of time, and they might be certain that the question of the election would be our fiscal relations. All he asked of his supporters was that they should work hard, not forgetting that on previous occasions they nearly achieved a victory. (Cheers.) He claimed to represent a "cause" and no personal interests, and one of the objects of his candidature would be to make one section of the community to think better of the other and to promote the brotherhood of man. (Loud cheers.)

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
DAMAGING A GAS METER AT WIDNES.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Police Court, Patrick Fitzgerald, 4, Marsh-street, was summoned by the Widnes_ Corporation for doing damage to a slot gas meter. He was fined 10s. and costs, and ordered to pay the damage.

div.head: LICENSING CHANGES AT WIDNES.
div.p: LICENSING CHANGES AT WIDNES.

At the Widries Police Court, on Thursday, Mr. J. W. Knowles applied for the following transfers, which were granted :—Hammer and Pincers, Hough Green, from S. G. Owens to John Robinson; Railway Inn, Victoria road, from John Robinson to Daniel Brennan; and the Crown Vaults, Ann-street West, from Daniel Brennan to J. S. Durkin. WIDNES MAGISTRATE AND OBSCENE LA.NGUAG E.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Police Court, Williatn. Flood, Longtons-row, Farnvvorth, and Fred Manifold, Carlyle-street, pleaded guilty to having created a breach of the peace.—Police-Constable Cleal in his evidence stated that the defendants were using obscene language, and the chairman (Mr, B. Brown) expressed the opinion that in cases like these the offenders ought to be pro- ceeded against for using obscene language.—They were each bound over for three months to keep the peace.

div.head: TKE RUNCORN W FLUE LEAD COMPANY.
div.p: TKE RUNCORN W FLUE LEAD COMPANY.

In the Vacation Court on Wednesday, Mr. Justice Walton appointed Mr. Kirby receiver and manager of the undertaking of the Runcorn White Lead Company. The action was by debenture-holders, who sought to enforce their security on the ,ground that the company had passed a resolution for a voluntary winding-up. By agreement, the motion was treated as the trial.

div.head: RUNCORN NE'ER-DO-WELL.
div.p: A RUNCORN NE'ER-DO-WELL.

At Runcorn, on Wednesday, Charles Whittle, a well- known character, was charged with being on the pre- mises of Mr.E. Monks, grocer, Penketh-lane, for an unlawful purpose. Detective Wilding in the early hours of yesterday morning, found the prisoner in the hayloft of Mr. Yfonks's stables. He had a pipe, matches, and tobacco in his possession. The magistrates com- mented on the danger involved, and sentenced prisoner to fourteen days' hard labour.

div.head: FARM LABOURER'S ATTEMPT AT SUICIDE.
div.p: FARM LABOURER'S ATTEMPT AT SUICIDE.

At Broxton Occasional Con-rt, on Wednesday, James Kelly, farm labourer, a native of Widnes, was charged with attempting to commit suicide at Edgeley, Ma'pas, on the 17th inst. The evidence was to the effect that prisoner was in the employ of Mr. William Windsdr, of Edgeley, and on Monday his employer sent him to Wrexham with a bull for sale. The animal was not sold, and prisoner returned intoxicated about 8.30. He hada quarrel in the kitchen, and threatened to throw his master down. Leaving the house, he remarked to Mr. Windsor's nephew, "I am going to end my life," and forthwith jumped into a pit near the farm. He . was rescued by a fellow labourer, and, after making an attempt to go to another pit, he was secured and taken to the barn. Caroline Jones, dom3stic servant at the farm, said prisoner had been keeping company with her, and he told her it was all through love. Prisoner, who seemed to regret his rash act, was remanded.

div.head: FUNERAL, OF A RUNCORN FOOTBALLER.
div.p: FUNERAL, OF A RUNCORN FOOTBALLER.

On Sunday afternoon the remains of the late Fletcher Gayter, a popular member of the Runcorn Football Club whose painfully sudden death from apoplexy was recorded last week, were interred in the Runcorn Cemetery. The funeral cortege was headed by sixty to seventy members of the Mersey Watermen's Union, with Mr. J. ! .Banner' vice-president, and Mr. E. Galley, secretary. These were fol- lowed by the committee officials and members of the Football Club, sixty-two in number. The com- mittee and officials included Messrs. W. Jones (chair- man), G. Robinson (vice-chairman), T. C. Price, H. Cawley, W. E. Dudley, H. Grounds, A. Abel, R. Briscoe, C. Powall (treasurer), J. Ellison (secretary), and A. Abel (assistant secretary). St. Edward's Brass Band, which includes several fellow workmen of deceased, also walked, and on the way to the cemetery played the Dead March. The officiating, clergyman was the Rev. W. Scholes. The bearers were four men.bers of the football team, four members of the Watermen's Union, ! and four from the Grate Warehouse. Wreaths were sent ! by Mr. T. Gayter and Mr. J. GAyter (brothers), Mr. J. ! Richardson and friends, and Mr. W. Maidens (cousin.) ! The Football Club also sent a handsome wreath. DEPARTURE OF' TILE REV. J. OSBORNE.

The Rev. J. Osborne, pastor of Bethesda Congrega- tional Church, Runcorn, left on Wednesday to commence his new pastorate at Commercial-street Congregational Church, Southampton. Preaching a farewell sermon on Sunday evening from the text "Far be it from me to glory save in the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ," he said ministers had their temptations, subtle and power- ful, the temptation to win popularity and the applause of the multitude, to say things that delighted the shallow ears of people, to degrade•the pulpit to the stump orator's level. Many a time they found that a con- gregation would turn away from a sober and thoughtful address or sermon ana would go into ecstasies over mere wordiness, "the trick of doing nothing with an air." He hoped he had not abused the name of our Lord by such devices. Then again ministers had their temptations in the financial side of their churches. He meant the temptation to make money the end of the ministry and to boast about the financial prosperity of the Church. They had not been able to boast much on that side but they had gone through very hard times when it would have paid them to pander to the many interests of the Church. A man might be forgiven for giving way to this temptation. Bread and butter, the needs of a family, were sometimes almost the main issue. He hoped he had never sold the Gospel even for bread and butter. Their chief glory-should be the setting forth of the Gospel of the Cross of Christ. He believed the Cross to be the only cure for sin and the one solace for human pain and sorrow. God so loved the world that He gave His Son. All their hopes lay there, the hope for time and eternity.—An open P.S.A. servicewas held in the afternoon, when Mr. Osborne presented a number of book prizes.—Mr. Osborne bade farewell to his congregation at a public social on Tuesday evening. The reverend gentleman was presented with a marble timepiece and a purse of gild from the congregation,a handsome barometer from the P.S.A., and a framed photo from the young men's class.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
PETE CURRAN AT EARLESTOWN.

On Saturday evening Mr.. Pete Curran, the well- known labour speaker, addressed a poorly-attended meeting of gasworkers and general labourers at the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, Earlestown. The Rey. H. Dunnico, of Warrington.presided. In his speech Mr. Curran deplored the small attethdance, and illustrated how efforts which would have beneficialresults for gas- workers and labourers were nsped in the bad and frustrated owing to the poor numbers in the local branch of the union. He contended that the ameliora- tion of the disadvantageous conditions under which the working class were labouring now would never take place unless the working mencombined together to fight for a fair day's wage for a fair day's labour.

div.head: NEW SCHOOLS NEAR HAYDOCK,
div.p: NEW SCHOOLS NEAR HAYDOCK,

• The Right Rev. D. Whiteside, Roman Catholic Bis- hop, of Liverpool, laid the memorial stone of a new industrial school of girl' k which is being ere3ted at a cost of £lO,OOO, at Blackbrook, near Haydock on Sun- day.aftemoon. The 'building will be of red brick and Runcorn stone, and will accommodate between 120 and 150 girls. The contractors are Messrs. Roberts and Robertson, of Liverpool, and the architects Messrs. Pugin and Pugin, of Liverpool and London. The new building will snrplant a temporary school, of which the Sisters of the Sacred Heart have been in charge for the past three years.. The weather on Sunday afternoon was gloriously fine, and there was a large attendance of the clergy and laity from the surrounding district, including Hayclock, Ashton, St. Helens, Wigan and other places.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ST. HELENS CORPORA.TEON LUNCHEONS.

At the meeting of the St. Helens 1-i-ighZis--Ci)mmittee on Wednesday adiscussion arose on a bill from the Town Hall keeper for some luncheons supplied to the committee. Councillor Hatton said there were con- fectioners and caterers in the town who would submit estimates for the luncheons—The Chairman replied that the luncheons were only chargcd at the cost to the hall keeper which was cheaper than anyone else could do it —Councillor Green said their was a great deal of feeling among the confectioners and caterers. They said they were ratepayets, and helped to pay the hallkeeper,s salary, and it was not fair that he should be placed in competition against them—rile surveyor said that when the luncheons were inaugurated they used to get some one in the town to cater; but they became expensive, and they let their own riiin provide—After some further discussion it was decided to refer the matter to the Parl iimentary Committee.

div.head: HELENS LABOURER'S STRANGF. DEATH.
div.p: HELENS LABOURER'S STRANGF. DEATH.

At St. Helens on Tuesday, an inquest was held on Edward Creighton, a labourer. Deceased had beeniun- ployed at Messrs. Cannington, Shaw, and Co.'s Sherdley Glass Bottle Works for the past six or seven years. Up to Wednesday last he had always regularly followed his work,and hadgood health. • On returning from work on the evening of that day he complained of vio- lent pains in his stomach. Homely remedies were tried. On the following day he complained to his landlady that on the previous Satur- day he had overlifted himself while at Work, and to this ha attributed his illness. As he bname worse, Dr. Masson was called in on Sunday morning, but he died, as stated on Monday. Dr. Masson, Who had made a post-mortem examination, now stated that in the abdomen there was a mass of tubercular glands, and ex- tending from . them was an ulceration which had eaten through the coat of the bowel and allowed the contents to escape in the peritoneum cavity. Death was due to septic peritonitis. In reply to the coroner, the doctor said there was no evidence that the man had received injury, and the jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

Cricket. Saturday was a blank date for local cricketers the miserable weather preventing indulgencein the pas- time. Enthusiasts will be pleased to learn that on Tues- day the Lancashire County Committee offered, a place in the Lancashire team which will meet Leicestershire next week to E: Gibson, a medium-pace left-hand bowler who has done good service for Warrington, but who has for the past two seasons been acting as professional to the Norfolk County Club, The offer has been accepted. Gibson's good, work recently against London County and the .11.0. C-14 wickets for 112 runs—has been the means of his being tried for his native county.

Mr. Gibson gives every promise of a successful career in the cricket world and his recent achievements have been noted with satisfaction by his numerous Warrington friends. Playing agninst W.. G. Grace's London County team on August 7th he bowled in admirable style and maintained a capital length. In the second innings he captured 6 wickets for 32 runs and his analysis for the match was 13 Wickets for 67 runs. Mr.- Gibson gave a capital account of himself in the second day's match. Seven wickets for 35 runs was his performance in the first innings and ha captured 6 wickets for 32 runs in the second innings. Throughout -the week Gibson bowled splendidly, bat his finest bag was against" W.G.'s ' side. In•all, he took 2:i wickets at the small cost of less than 7 runs per wicket. Doubtless his only regret was that he had n t the dis- tinction of b)wling. the red mbtable " W.G.," wh o was dismissed by J.N. Worman. •

Mr. Gibson added m•lre 'laurels to his name in the encounter with AMC. at Lords, capturing 5 wickets for 41 runs. This we his father was gratified to receive a letter stating that on Saturday he had an interview wittr•Macharen, who wanted him to have a trial as he was goink to ask the Lancashire Committee to put him on the side against Leicester on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday next: As we have already stated the Committee agreed to include Mr. Gibson in the eleven. •

The writer had an interview with Mr. Gibson's father who is naturally very proud of his SOll'S per- formances in the field. lie recounted with pleasure the time when his son's services were sought after, by various junior teams. and said that often there would be representatives of several organizations waiting to secure his help at the week-end. Mr. Gibson played for the Warrington eleven about two years and showed himself to be a bowler of no mean ability. There should be some Warrington spectators at the County match next week! .

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.
T. Astill, of Warrington, ;on the second Prize in tlae mile bicycle handicap at Congleton Sports on Saturday, being beaten by three lengths by J. Banks, of Congletoa, whom he conceded 13 yards start.

Wretched weather 'marred the • enjoyment of the fifteen members of the Worington Cycling Club who visited ,Chester last Saturday on the occasion of "President's Day." In accordance with a time- honoured custom the esteemed President (Mr. John Naylor) was entertained by the club. All had to make the journey to Chester by train, and .on arrival the time waS 'whiled away by a stroll round the interesting Rows. T4ater, capital tea was.provided by Host Riley ,of the Hop Pole Hotel, and, needless to say, was thoroughly en- joyed. After tea, the captain (Mr. W. Taylor) cor- dially welcomed the President (Mr. John Naylor) on behalf of the club, the Hon. Sec. (Mr. E. Piciavance) and Mr. D. Davies supplementing his remarks with a : few well-chosen words. Mr. Naylor, in replying, paid a warm tribute to the Warrington Cycling Club, and referred to his ever increasing interest in its welfare. He wished the members every success. The rain having now ceased, the party adjourned to Capiter's boat house, where a specially chartered steamer was in waiting. The sail up the beautiful Dee was greatly appreciated. Chester was reached just as the rain was again falling, so that a general move was made to the station. Warrington was reached without mishap at about 10.0 p. m.

div.head: Rugby Football.
div.p: Rugby Football.

Practic3s for ,the ra,pidly-approaching season have been held on several evenings lately, and some of the men are showing their best form already. Two new forwards have already appeared, viz., G. Thomas of Newport; and Jones of Birkenhead, a Cheshire County scrammager about 13 stone weight. Boat are con- sidered good captures. There will be a full side practice on the football ground this evening.

Jim Valentine on Tuesday evening informed the Swinton officials that he had finally decided to retire. His career with the" Lions" commenced in the season 18834, and his most successful season was 1888-9, when he sowed 48 tries and kicked 17 goals. He represented his country on four occasions, and was selected twice in addition wh3n the international dis- putes took place. Besides this he captained Lanca- shire for ten years consecntively. Last season he led the Swinton" A " team to vicbry in the Lancashire Combination. Something in the shape of a testimonial to commemorate his retirement should be organised.

div.head: HATTON HORTICULTURAL SHOW.
div.p: HATTON HORTICULTURAL SHOW.

The ninth annual show in connection with the Hatton Horticultural Society was held on Thursday afternoon, and unfortunately the weather was of the most unfavourable description. This was to be regretted, as the promoters had worked hard to organize a successful exhibition, and generous public patronage was hoped for. As was to be expected under the circumstances there were not many visitors to the show from War- rington and district but there was a fairly good attend- ance of residents of the village. The show was held in two large marquees erected ma field kindly lent by Mr. James Parr and although the number of exhibits showed a slight decrease on previous years, the qtality reached an exceptionallyhigh standard. The collection of vegetables was a very creditable one. The show was opened by Miss Whitley, the Rev. F Clifton Smith presiding over the ceremony. Miss Whitley expressed her sorrow that they were experiencing sucha wet day. It was scarcely necessary for her to say how pleased she was to be once more among her friends at Hatton, especially on an occasion like that. Those local flower shows did a great amount of good in effecting a love for and an improvement in the cultivation of flowers and vegetables, and in Hatton such an improvement had been brought about in the quality of the flowers and vegetables grown that she felt they could not repay the debt of gratitude which they I owed to the Horticultural Society. (Applause) The Rev. R. Clifton Smith proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Whitley for her services. in consequence of the rain he did not expect that the show would be a success financially, but happily they had a reserve fund to fall back upon. He trusted that next year they would have fine weather—(hear, hear)—and that the Society would continue to prosper. (Applause.) Mr. James Parr seconded the motion which was heartily carried, Miss Whitley briefly responding. Mr. Parr was also thanked for the use of the field. An interesting ceremony then took place. For many years the hon. secretary of the society Mr. J.O. Hatton, has worked assiduously on the society's behalf. Ills efforts were fittingly recognized by the members, who presented him with a beautiful marble clock. The gift was handed to Mr.lHatton by Miss Whitley. Mr. Hatton thanked the donors of the gift for their present, and assured all that in the past he had only done his duty, a thing he was prepared to do as long as he was connected with the society. The judgeg, whose decisioes gave every satisfaction were:—Farmers' produce, Messrs. Joseph Knowles and. Edwin Britch; cottagers' gardens and produce, Messrs; Edward Slater and John V. Smith; honey, Mr. H. Potts, butter and eggs, Miss Baxter; table decbrations, Lady Greenall, Mrs. J. J. Whitley and Mrs. John White; and j baskets of wild flowers, Mrs. Fletcher and Mrs. Bower. Beautiful collections of hothouse plants and flowers had been sent by Sir Gilbert Groeuall, Mr. .T. H. Lyon and Mrs. Massey ; and Mr. Cartwright, of Moore, exhibited Some honey. During the afternoon the Preston Brook Brass Band gave selections of music. _

div.head: CHRIST CHURCH, PADGATE. Rain Spoils the Garden Fete.
div.p: CHRIST CHURCH, PADGATE. Rain Spoils the Garden Fete.

The elements were in their worst mood on Thursday, and one could hardly imagine a more unsuitable day for an outdoor function. From early morning until the evening rain, fell in a continuous, steady downpour, and to say the least the conditions were most depressing. One could not help sympathising with the Padgate Church workers, who had arranged the annual garden fête in aid of various parochial organizations for that day: Certainly the best course would have been to have postponed the event, but, no doubt in hopes of an improvement later in the, dab. it was decided in. the morning that the fête should proceed as usual. The pretty Vicarage-grounds were again placed at the disposal of the congregation, and several marquees were, erected for the. accommoda... Mott of the stalls and side shows. Theretwas a capital display of useful and fancy wares, ands nicely arranged refreshment stall. The following were the stallholders and assistants :—Fancy stall, Mrs. Pollock Hill, assisted by Mrs. Royston, Mrs. Joseph Bennett, Miss Boyd and. Miss K. Birtles; basket and pottery stall, Mrs. J. D. Bitekton ;. refreshment stall,Miss Jackson, assisted by Mesdames Denham, Riggall, and Fryar, and the Misses D. Royston, M. Warburton, A. Btrchall, E. Royston, A. Birtles and Houghton; rummage stall; Miss Bower- ing, assisted by Mesdames Blackwell, Hatton, and London, Misses Wood and Brimelow; fish pond, Miss F. Holt; toy stall, Miss L. Birtles; tobacco stall, Miss A. Horridge.

There was a fair attendance at the opening ceremony, which was performed by Miss.-Egerton Warburton of Arley Hall. The Vicar (Rev. W. Pollock Hill), who has been confined to the house through illness for several weeks, was fortunately sufficiently recovered to be able to attend, and as usual presided. There were also present the. Rev. G. Vale-Owen (curate-. in-cbmge of Orford Church), the Rev. Lewis Richardson (vicar of Binley, near Coventry), Colonel J. D. Buckton (vicar's warden). Mr. G. Mather (people's warden), Mr. G. Blackwell (treasurer of the Fête Committee) and others. At the ontset Miss Egerton Warburton was presented by Miss Irene Bennett with a lovely bouquet of sweet peas and maiden hair fern tied with pink ribbon.

The Vicar said he could assure Miss Egerton Warbur- ton that she would receive a very hearty welcome because they felt doubly grateful to her for coming to help them under the—he was .going t,o say painful— circumstances of such a very wet day. She had driven about ten and a half miles to keep her engagementlan4 he felt certain all present would appre- ciate her kindness. In regard to the objects of the sale they generally had seven or eight objects to support. Last year they helped the Church House, Mothers' Meeting, Ladies Sewing Meeting, the Church House Library. Churchwardens' funds, Woolston school, and the Padgate School building 'fund. About £45 was handed over to the building fund, and the schools had since been erected. As a result of last year's sale they had a balance of £B4 to -divide among the objects he had named. The year before they had an exceedingly goodsale, the proceeds amounting to no less than £lOB. He was afraid that owing to the bad weather they would have to come down another step this year: Re believed that as the first occasion on which Miss Egerton War- burton had performed the opening :ceremony at such a function, and he could only hope it would .not be the last by any means. He felt sure that as in the past she had often given a very good lead to the ladies in the, hunting field in Cheshire, she would perform that open- ilor ceremony in a manner worthy of general imitation. (Applause). Miss Egerton Warburton, who was cordially received, said it was a great pleasure to her to come to Padgate and take part in their garden fete. She only wishedshe 'could have brought with her the sunshine which they had all wished for so much. The fete was becoming an annual institutiOn and a great deal seemed to have been done in the parish already. She had heard of the energetic activity of the Padgate people in building the Church Hous% which was opened some few years ago and the new infant school which had been erected at a cost of £7OO after several years of patient work. All this seemed the more wonderful, as Padgate did not abound in millionaires. (Laughter.) She was sure the increasing needs of the parish made it necessary that the fete should be an annual institution, and it deserved their heartiest good wishes. It must be the outcome of what was better than wealth—sympathy, kindness, :Lnd true interest in the work of the Church. (Applause.)

Colonel Bucktou proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Egerton Warburton and said he was sure they all appre- ciated her kindness and the interest she had shown in Padgate by attending. He had no doubt that the sale would go on all right in spite of the bad weather. He thought they all felt to some extent specially indebted to the Vicar for Miss Warburton's attendance. That WaS perhaps the first time the Vicar had appeared in public for a, month and they were very glad to see that he was better and able to take part in an event which he had so much at heart.
Mr. G. Mather seconded and said their thanks were doubly due to Miss Warburton for braving the elements to attend the fate.

The motion was heartily agreed to and In resOnding the Vicar said they .had looked for- ward to the fete _being a great improvement .on last year's because so riviny people had interested them- selves in providing extra side shows and improving the ordinary stalls. • - The business of the sale then commenced.

Numerous attractions had been provided, not the least interesting being the competitions which excited considbrable amusement. There was an ingeniously- contrived shooting gallery, in charge of Messrs. Chambers, Boyd, and Pocock, and ladies and gentlemen tried their skill at shooting with 'air guns. The various competitions resulted as follows :—Ladies' air gun shooting competition: Ist prize, Mrs. Chambers; 2nd prize, Miss N. Houghton. Gentlemen's hat trimming competition : Ist, Mr. S. Atkinson; 2nd, Mr. E. Atkinson. Ingenuity prize; Mr. Chambers. Gentle- men's air gun shooting competition: Ist, Rev. W. Pollock-Hill; 2nd, Mr. S. Atkinson; 3rd, Mr. J. Fryar. Ladies' washing competition : Ist, Miss E. Walsh ; 2nd, Mrs. Gorton. Gentlemen's washing competition i : Ist, Mr.-Horrocks; 2nd, Mr. E. Atkinson. At intervals Professor A. Horrocks gave very clever exhibitions of shadowgraphv and chapeaugraphy which were well patronized. In the evening the IVarrington Volunteer Band under the conductorship of Mr. ..J. T. Richardson, was in attendance and played an excellent programme; and at the close dancing was 'indulged in in the large marquee. The grounds were beautifully illumimated with fairy lamps which had been arranged by Mr. H. Hoult. the general arrangements had been, admirably carried out by a committee, presided over by the Vicar with Mr. Blackwell as treasurer.
The attendance in the evening showed a decided improvement, and the day's proceeds amounted to about.
