div.p: WARRINGTON

THE BENEFITS OF SCIENCE. It is seldom that any discovery of science is such as will benefit all classes of people. Some of the greatest discoveries of the age, while they have proved directly oeneficial to thousands, have also, at least for a time, injured other thousands. Even some of the best medi- cinal preparations, however much they may do to remove one class of disease, or suit some constitutions, at the same time either deepen the hold of another disease, or leave it entirely untouched, or if they bengit one class of patients, they. may injure another. Now the great need of the age is some scientifically arranged preparation which will cope effectually with the prevalent diseases of this country, which will be certain to do good when fairly tried, which will be equally adapted to the needs of the mer- chant and the workman, the professional man, and he who wins his bread by the sweat of his brow, the student, the clerk, the factory hand, the miner, and the roadside labourer. It should be, too, such a preparation a contains no injurious ingredients, and which may be taken with impunity by the weakly child, or the delicate lady, as well as by the stronger constituted man. Such a discovery would deserve to be called The Perfection of Medicinal Preparations, and would indeed be an Invaluable Boon to Suffering Humanity. Now this much needed boon has been found, has been tried, has been proved, and wherever proved, it has been found satisfactory. We refer to Gwilym Evans' Quinine Bitters, the Vegetable Tonic, which when once tried, has been always recommended, and has proved successful when all other medicine has failed to give rerief, and we may say further, that it has proved permanently beneficial, when other pre- parations at best only gave temporary relief. It is strongly recommended as The Best ftemek of the Age for Indigestion in its different forms, such as Sick Headache, Pains in the Side, Giddiness, Loss of Appe- tite, also for Nervousness and Nervous Disorders, Sleep- lessness, Neuralgia, Low Spirits and all kinds of , Weakness. It has often proved very beneficial to persons suffering from great Weakness either after an illness, long confinement to ill-ventilated rooms or any other cause. It strikes at the source of the Disease, removing the cause of the illness, and strengthens those parts as the system which have been weakexed by it, .and therefore most liable to colds and other ailments. Gwilym Evans' Quinine Bitters being purely vegetable, it is a. Natural Tonic, and suited to all ages at all seasons of the year. It is everywhere acknowledged to be a powerful aid in restoring the body to a healthy state when deranged by disease. div.head: CHANGES OF MARRIAGE. A St. Helens Bride of Seventeen.
div.p: CHANGES OF MARRIAGE. A St. Helens Bride of Seventeen.

According to the Registrar General's returns, actresses stand the best chance of marriage, domestic servants come a good second, and typists are well up le the list. Governesses are almost the ' last in the ranks, teachers and shop assistants are about equal, and lady clerks and dressmakers each have a good chance of securing eligible partners. Very few factory girls languish in single blessedness: but nurses do not marry so readily as might be supposed. Girls in the colliery districts marry ea.rlier than the majority of our English maidens. Nineteen is quite an average age for girls, eighteen and seventeen very ordinary, while, occasionally, girls of fifteen are led to the altar. A representative of the "St. Helens Reporter" recently had a most instructive interview with a Mrs. Rigby, a collier's wife, who was married when she was seventeen years of age. Mrs. Rigby, who had been married two years, lives at 18, Baker- street,, St. Helens. Had mai enjoyed good health. , her married life would have been a most happy one However thanks to Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people, Nlrs. Rigby is now well and strong. Mrs. Rigby said :—" My husband is at present employed at the Ashton Green Colliery, and, as you See, we have one child.* Before I was married, I was comparatively healthy, though I.sometimes suffered from pains in the head. After my baby was born, however, T began to feel weak and low-spirited. A doctor attended me for two months, during the whole of which time I lay in bed, suffering a good deal of pain, which was something like windy spasms. After a time I was able to get up, but, though the pain had gone, I was not the same woman, getting out of breath very easily. The dostor's advice was that I should walk in the open-air as much as possible, but I had no inclination to go out-of-doors because of the baby. " I am now better, thanks to Dr. Williams' pink pills. My mother happened to be in the shop of Norbury, greengrocer, one day, when a young .woman there in- quired about me. My mother described to her what my complaint was like, and the young woman at once said 'I was a bit like that myself at one time,and I took Dr. Williams' pink pills, and they did me a world of good. We at once bought a box, and by the time I had taken the contents I felt much stronger, and better in every i way. I_ took several boxes of the pills and now feel excellent.

div.head: DOUBLE DROWNING FATALITY.
div.p: DOUBLE DROWNING FATALITY.
A Boy's Fatal Gallantry at Latchford.

Peculiarly distressing are the circumstances surround- ing the death of two LAtchford boys who were drowned in the Bridgewater Canal on Wednesday evening. It appears that three boys named John Handford Corbett, aged nine, son of Mr. Jos .ph Rowland Corbett, of 9. Belmont-avenue, Latchford: John Hodgson Wilson, aged 10, son of Mr. William John Wilson, G. Lyon- street; and a companion named Acton. were playing on the wooden turn-bridge which spans the Bridgewater Canal near Black Bear Bridge when Corbett fell into the water Wilson at once divested himself of his contend jump- ing into the canal made a gallant attempt to rescue his friend. Unfortunately both boys sank and before assist- ance was forthcoming they were drowned. The bodies were recovered shortly after by a man named Joseph Lowe, a Runcorn boat captain. Artificial respiration was applied for nearly an hour, but unfortunately with- out avail, and Dr. Smith, who as summoned to the spot, pronounced Life to be extinct. The bodies were removed to the homes of the parents. Mr. Corbett is very well known in Warrington, having recently con- ducted a series of mission services in the Parr Hall. Much sympathy is felt with him and with Mr. Wilson in their painfully sudden bereavement. It is onlya few weeks ago that the boy Wilson was success- ful in•saving a boy from drowning. in a pit. at Latch- ford and he was shortly to receive the Royal Humane Society's award for his gallantry. It is indeed sad to think that at so early an ago his life should have been sacrificed in an attempt to save another.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.

SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. Birchall (presiding), IL T. Fairclough, J. W. Hayward and Dr. Fox. A DISORDERLY WOMAN.—EIIen Caldwell, Winwick street, was sent to gaol for a month for having been guilty of disorderly conduct in the market place on Friday evening, and assaulting P. C. Clough.—Clough had occasion to take the prisoner into custody and Site then became very violent and struck him several times in the chest. SOLDIER IN TROUBLE.—Thomas Fitzgerald, a soldier Iron). Orford Barracks, was charged with stealing four military blankets, of the value of 205.,0n Friday night. —Sergeant Smith was in Gorsey lane at about mid- night and saw the prisoner standing near a doorway concealing the blankets. He questioned him and prisoner said he had taken the blankets to enable him to sleep out all night. He was not going to make away with them.A. sergeant from the barracks said there were numerous complaints about blankets and other things being missed. Prisoner had been in the service eight years andhad just returned from India. He had a.very good character.—The magistrates dismissed the case. SLEEPING °VT.—Rose Taylor and Florence Jaundrell were charged with sleeping out at the Barracks on Friday evening.—The case was adjourned sine die, the girls promising to go to a home. MoNDAY.—Before Mr. Monks (in the chair), Messrs. Birchall, and Wright, Alderman Smethurst, and

Councillor Thornton. MINOR CASES.—John Longsbaw, greengrocer, Mill- street, and Joseph Bullock, contractor, Alder-lane, were charged with fighting in Bewsey-street on the 6th August, and were bound over to keep the peace and ordered to pay the costs, 7s. each.—Thomas Burke hawker, Knowles's-yard, for fighting in Turner-street, was similarly dealt with.—A fine of 20s. was imposed. on Alwyn Jenks, foreman, Welch's-yard, for making use of obscene language in the Old-road.—Frank M'Cciy, carter, Sloop-yard, was fined ss. for using a horse and cart in Liverpool-road at 11.20 p.m., without having a lighted lamp attached to the vehicle. AssAxims ON POLICENIEN.—WiIIiam Butler, 2, Buck- ley-street, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Knutsford-road at 8.50 on Sunday night and with assaulting P.C. Clarke.--It appeared on being taken into custody for drunkenness prisoner became very violent and kicked and butted the officer. With the assistance of Constables Heap and Johnson he was taken to the Police Station.—A fine of 10s. was im- posed.—George Prince was fined 10s. for having been drunk and disorderly in Museum-street at 12.45 a.m. on Sunday and assaulting Constables Bennett and Tolly.
TUESDAY.—Before Dr. Fox (in the chair) and

Mr. Birchall. To BE COURT-MARTI A.M. ED —Wi Ili(Lin Thomas Dickenson, newsagent, Scotland road, was charged with having whilst serving with the colours in January, .stolen a sum of money belonging to the military authorities' from Orford Barracks—Superintendent Monaghan stated that in January prisoner was serving as a sergeant at Orford Barracks and subsequently went nn the reserve. Shortly after he left money and other property were missed and on Monday the military authorities took out a warrant against the prisoner who was arrested by Detective Forster and P.C.Leonard. He the superintendent) asked the magistrates to hand the prisoner over to the military authorities to be dealt with by the court martial—This course was adopted. WEITSESD A Y.—Be fOre Mr. T. Birchall (presiding) and

Aldermen Hutchinson and Monks. STOLEN ARTICLES PLEDGED.—WARNING TO PAWN- IIROKF.Rs.—A woman named Elizabeth Duckworth, of no fixed address, was charged with stealing a quilt and a sheet, of the value of 55., the property of William Rogerson, 8, Cropper's-brow.—Superintendent Mona- ghan stated that about six weeks ago prisoner and a man went to lodge at prosecutor's house. After being there about a fortnight prisoner went to live in one of Mr. lOgerson's cottages opposite, and the articles in question were lent to her. Whet' prosecutor went to see the prisoner on Tueslay to give her notice to leave he found the quilt and sheet were missing. He (the super- intendent) subsequently discovered the articles had bowl pledged at Messrs. Jackson's pawnshop. Stamped on each of them were the following words: "This is stolen from W. Rogerson's Warrington." When charged; with the theft prisoner replied" Yes, I took them, and pledged them. '—Prisoner wars sentenced to one month's imprisonment.—Questioned by the Chairman, the pawn- broker's assistant stated that he did not notice the marks on the articles or he would certainly not have advanced money on the:la.—As it was he advanced 4s.— The Chairman observed that that showed the necessity or taking more care.—On Superintendent Managhan's application, the Bench ordered the things to be returned to Rogerson, the Chairman remarking that it would teach the pawnbroker to be more careful. ' Frtroa.v.—Before Mr. Hepherd (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillors John Roberts, and Thornton. A TRIVIAL CAm—A boy named Joseph Britton, 18, Hind street, was summoned by another boy named Joseph Stout, 34, Hind street for assaulting him on the 16th inst—Cornplainant said that he and some other boys were playing at cricket in the street and the ball struck the defendant who then struckcomplainant in the face with his fist.—The Chief Constable • said the boys had no right to be playing at cricket in the street on Sunday—The Chairman said the case was a trumpery one and would be dismissed. ALLEGED WIFE ASSAULT.—James Stirrup, Admiral street, did not appear to answer to a summons charging him with assaulting his wife, Mary A. Stirrup, on the 11th inst.—Complainant alleged that defendant struck her in the mouth with his cap. He then seized a poker and threatened to cut her head off, and she was obliged to leave the house.—The Bench granted a warrant for the ,defendant's apprehension.

div.head: Warrington County Petty Sessions.
div.p: Warrington County Petty Sessions.
America Too
MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S
ATTACK ON FREE TRADE.
[BY A CORREsroN i)ENT.]

WHY has Mr. Chamberlain suddenly sprung this attack upon Free Trade. on the country? If anybody had told us in March last that before the summer was here we should all have been tremendously in earnest over defending or attacking Free Trade we should have laughed at them. How is it, then, that what seemed absurd even to imagine last spring is an accomplished fact to-day ? We most of us know, to our sorrow, that changes in our national life come slowly enough. Think of

any half-dozen political and social reforms we are interested in, and then look back to the day when those reforms were first demanded. Why, it is' ages ago. Only the greybeards among us can remember those days when the reformers of the middle of the last century fought so stoutly for principles which we have ' no A, at last begun to recognise as the founda- tion of practical politics. How is it, then, that Mr. Chamberlain has been able in the space of a few short months to turn almost - the whole political thought and interest of the country out of its natural course into an entirely different direction ?

Hence Mr. Chamberlain was forced to abandon any present-day programmes, and to turn back into the pages of ancient history for an electioneering cry. He discovered at last the old "Protection" cry that did such good service for the Tories a hundred- years ago. This be dressed up in some new Imperial clothes and took it down to show his faithful friends in Birmingham. Birmingham was one of the places that killed Protection in the old days, so perhaps Mr. Chamberlain thought if he could make them believe in Birmingham that Protection dressed in Imperial clothes was a new and wonderful discovery of his own, which would revive trade and bind the Empire together in a manner never heard of before, theo there was a good chance of making the resi of the country think the same.

WELL, on May 25th he produced his Imperial Protection to a few select Birming- ham friends. He told them there that he had bees on the "illimitable veldt" of South Africa, and, he had breathed a new air. He had learnt to , see much further than he had seen before, Wand the result was that when he came home, everything we were interested in -seemed very small and parochial. We had been getting excited over EducaKon and other matters of no importance. But he was going to teach us to forget all about those things, and turn our attention to far more important things across the seas. When the election came we were to forget all about education because he Ivould find us something far more important to talk about. Here are his words: I do not think that a General Election is near. Ent whether it is near or distant, I think our opponents may perhaps find that the issues ,vl.,ch they propose to raise are not the issues on which we shall take the opinion of the country.. It we raise an issue of this kind, the answer will not depend upon petty personal considerations, nor upon temporary interests, but upon whether the people of this country really have it in their heart s to do all that is necessary to consolidate an Empire that can only be maintained by relations of interest as well as by relations of ' sentiment.

LET us for the moment put out of our minds the thought that Mr. Chamberlain was putting forward what he hoped was a good patriotic election cry to cover up the inevitable defeat of the Government over the Education question. Let us forget all about that, and ask ourselves what it is that the Colonial Secretary wishes us to believe is his motive in bringing Protection forward again after all these years? He wishes us to believe that unless we are prepared to abandon Free Trade we must abandon the Colonies; or, rather, the abandonment of Free Trade is the rice the Colonies will ask for continuing to :remain within the Empire. Which, as Euclid ppm is absurd,

div.head: FATALITY TO A WIDNES LABOURER.
div.p: FATALITY TO A WIDNES LABOURER.

_ Mr. Samuel Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Accident Hospital, on Tuesday afternoon, touching the death of James Hoey, aged twenty-one years, Moss Bank-road, who was fatally burned on Friday at Messrs Sullivan's works. Deceased was engaged in the carbide shed, where he had charge of one of the furnaces, when, through some cause or another, it exploded, and covered the unfortunate man with the burning rnaterial.—Mr. Carey, assistant manager, with the aid of a model, gave a detailed account of the working of the furnace and the duties of the work man in charge. Ills (witness's) opinion of the cause of the explosion was that there may have been an accumulation of gas imprisoned under the surface, and this, getting to a high pressure' had burst. No accident had happened before ;In fact, the: never thought anything like the present case couldhappen. —After evidence of death had been given, the Coroner said he would like to make an inspection of the furnace. —Mr. •Saxby (his Majesty's Inspector), Mr. J. W. Knowles (representative for the United Alkali), and Mr. F. E. Poole (solicitor for the relatives) all agreed upon this course, and the inquest was adjourned until Wednesday next at a quarter-past two o'clock in the afternoon.

div.head: GARDEN CITY SCHEME, The Latest Developments.
div.p: THE GARDEN CITY SCHEME, The Latest Developments.

The Garden City Association is pursuing an energetic campaign, and before many months are over the first fruits of its activity will be seen in the creation of a Model village upon the principle laid down by the founder of the garden city movement. Besides the interest that has been displayed in the laying out of the future town at the naval base on the Forth, the association is, says a London correspondent, in active negotiation with the British Aluminium Company, who desire its co-operation in the laying out of a garden village for the workpeople employed at their factory at Foyers, on the Caledonian Canal, Inverness- shire. But the scheme which is nearest to accomplish- la,,ent will be carried out in the vicinity of London. The vioneer Company, which is in reality the active agent !If the association, has acquired an estate of 4,oooacres In the vicinity of Hitchin, Herts, about thirty-five 11\!lles out of London. It is situated on the Great orthern Railway main line, and is intersected by the h Ilelane to Cambridge. The land is of good agri- eult.ural quality and well suited for development, and ngmeers are at present considering how it should be ;Id out for a - town of 30,000 inhabitants. In ee course :.%f a few days a company will be °trued, with a capital of £300,000 of which a te;k:onsiderable proportion has already been promised by directors of the Pioneer Company and their friends. a th new company will then take over the estate from lt_e Pioneer Company and proceed with developments,l It is expected that actual operations may be corn- ' Wr"need in the early part of next year. Arrangements 4r: new being made with the first manufacturers who to transfer their factories from London to the new garden city.

DROWNING FATALITY.
Fatal Bathe at Widnes.

At Widnes Accident Hospital yesterday week, Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest on the body of Joseph Nulty, 7, Water-street, Widnes, who was drowned on the pre- vious Wednesday while bathing in the river Mersey.— William Devonport, 1, Water-street, said he was nine years of age. On Wednesday about live o'clock he with the deceased and two other boys were playing on the Widnes Marsh. Nulty took his clothes off and went into the water. He tried to walk across to Runcorn, but fell in a hole and disappeared. Witness did not see him again.—The Coroner explained that the boys clothes were found on the bank by tin engine driver, and the boys then told him what had happened and in- formation was given to the police.—Walter Stacey de- posed to having found the body on Thursday evening lower down the river than where the accident *took place.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was accidentally drowned.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday August 22, 1903. WORKINGMEN'S MISSION, BANK QUAY. LAYING THE FOUNDATION STONE OF THE NEW CHAPEL Mr. H. Roberts and Sectarianism.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday August 22, 1903. WORKINGMEN'S MISSION, BANK QUAY. LAYING THE FOUNDATION STONE OF THE NEW CHAPEL Mr. H. Roberts and Sectarianism.

The company then reiurned to the schoolroom where Captain Crosfield delivered a short speech. He had laid the stone, he said, in the hope that the same keenness and energy would be displayed beneath the roof and within the walls of the new chapel, as had been shown in the past in the old mission. He fully endorsed what the Chairnian had said with regard to non-sectarianism. He hoped that the mission workers would continue to display that broad, tolerant spirit which they had already manifested. Everything which tended to raise man above his lower nature was of the greatest benefit, and therefore all kinds of spiritual teaching were of benefit. Amongst the other precepts which would no doul:t be taught at the chapel, there were two which he would like to feel would have a promi nent place, and they were stout-heartedness and persist- ency. It was a very splendid thing to show a merry countenance in misfortune. The secretary had referred to the fact that the works were obliged to take the old mission room for extension purposes, and he said he knew the directors regretted having to take that course. That was perfectly true. The firm was getting bigger every day and if he thought it was going to end in nothing but being a big concern, he personally should not feel much enthusiasm about it. But he was sure. that each member of the firm now recognized that the success of the firm was the interest of every individual ' employ 4, no matter how humble, and he hoped that gradually as time went on and when it had come to be recognized more fully, the feeling of common interest would give such a sustained impetus that • they would igo on carrying everything before them,and not rest until they made ita firm where the health, happiness and comfort of everyone were assured. (Applause.) That was their idea, that was what they must all work for,and it was a very fine thing to see that some big firms had already ackieved it • and that they had spread the true and right sort of happiness around hem. He wished the mission workers every success ti their new under- taking, and hoped they would go In from strength to strength. (Applause.) The hymn "This stone to Thee in Juth we lay" was then sung and the band played ano er selection in admirable style. A collection was tak on behalf of the building fund and realized the han orne SLIM of £l46s.

Saturday was a red letter day in the history of the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay. Since 1871 the congregation has worshipped in the small chapel in Liverpool-road, erected by the late Mt. John Crosfield on a site adjoining the works of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited. It has now become necessary to further extend the works,and for this pur- pose the firm have had to acquire the chapel. The mission workers have lost no time in embarking upon a scheme for the erection of a new and more com- modious building and their efforts have received welcome support financially from ' Messrs. Crosfield and various friends. A site ; adjoining the handsome new schools in Thewlis- street has been selected and Saturday afternoon witnessed the laying of the foundation stone of the new chapel. The cost of the building, including a new organ, will be at least £1,200, so that the energies of the congregation will be taxed for some tithe to come in raising the necessary funds. A special effort in the shape of a bazaar will be put forth early in November. It is expected that the new chapel will seat about 320 persons as compared with 210 accom- modated in the old building. Plans have been pre- pared by Mr. R. M. Roberts, A.R.1.8.A., and Mr. George Wallington is being entrusted with the building of the chapel. , Although the weather on Saturday was very un- favourable the interesting proceedings attendant upon the laying of the foundation stone wbre carried out with a success which should augur well for tile future prosperity of the mission. Captain G. R. Crosfield laid the stone in the presence of a large assembly presided over by Mr. H. Roberts. Others present included— Mrs. Crosfield, Miss Truda Crosfield, Mrs. Roberts, Miss Roberts. Mr. R. M. Roberts, Councillors Burton, James Evans and Broiigh, Mr. G. Wallington and Mr. A. Tilling (hon. secretary). Owing to indisposition Miss Bessie Dutton was unable to attend but sent a donation to the Building fund. The proceedings com- menced with the march" Heroique " by the members of Crosfield's prize band who gave their services. The hymm " How lovely are Thy tents, 0 Lord !" was then sung, and Councilor W. Brough engaged in prayer. Mr. A. TILLING then announced that he had received a letter from Mr. A. H. Crosfield regretting his in- ability to attend as he would be away in Switzerland that day. Had he been in England he would have allowed nothing to interfere with his attending on so interesting an occasion and he was very glad to know that the family would be well represented. Mr. F. Monks, J.P., also wrote stating that he would be unable to be present as he would be out of town "We like to encourage" he continued "every effort, for the promotion of a self-elevating, religious com- munity, free from all priestly control. I am all the more pleased to see that the younger generation of the Crosfield family are taking their share in the responsi- bilities of this end of the town. I need not discuss the work Crosfield's have done for the town. The present and a recent gift bear ample testimony to their good- will." Letters had also been received from Dr. Markel, Councillor Tinnion Mr. Ridgway, solicitor, and Mr. C. E. Parker. Mr. William Worrall wrote on behalf of the Mission Society Class, stating that at the last meeting of the Society it was resolved that a sum of £5 be given to the Building fund as a thank offering at the ceremony of the foundation stone laying. Continuing, the hon. secretary said the old chapel was erected by the late Mr. John Crosfield in 1871, and the schools were added at the same gentle , man's expense a few years afterwards. Both the chapel and schools were built on land adjoining Messrs. Cros- field's works. When the firm became alimitedcompany the property was transferred to the company and taken out of Mr. Crosfield's hands to some extent. Almost immediately the schools were required for extension purposes, and Mr. Crosfield again came for- ward with his noble .generosity and built the handsome new building in which they were gathered that after- noon. Messrs. Crosfield had allowed them to worship in the old chapel free of charge, and they had to thank the company for their kindness, knowing that they had been very much inconvenienced for want of additional premises. He believed the firm had very reluctantly given them notice to remove from the chapel, and had promised a subscription of £3OO towards the building of the new chapel. (Applause.) Their thanks were also due to Mrs. Crosfield and the trustees for their kindness in allowing them to erect the new building in theschool yard. The chapel would be under a distinct trusteeship from the school, and would be entirely under the control of the worshippers, who would have the power orelect- lug the trustees. That power had, in fact, already been exercised, and a z list—of 21 trustees drawn up. The mission had all along been conducted on non- sectarian lines. That was the oft repeated request oi the founder and out of deference to his wishes a clause had been put in the trust deeds that the new building should for all time remain undenominational and unsectarian. In the past the pulpit had been filled mainly by the Independent Methodist friends. Tile new chapel would accommodate about 100 or 110 more , persons than the old one. Mr. R. M. Roberts had pre- pared the plans very admirably and they had a capable builder in Mr. Wallington. • Mr. John Hassell had kindly promised to act as clerk of works free of charge. In addition to the donation of £3OO promised by Messrs. Crosfield, £2OO had been promised by Mrs. Crosfield (£lOO for the building fund and £lOO for the organ fund), and £lO by Mr. H. Roberts who had also made himself responsible for the architect's fees. The men's class had guaranteed £5O apart from the effort they were making in connection with the bazaar It was hoped to obtain £3OO by means of the bazaar and other efforts would have to be put forth to raise the balance required. (Applause.) The CrtarnmAN said that in the first place they had two causes for regret. The first was the absence of Mr. Arthur Crosfield, whom everyone of them would have felt very delighted to have seen there, and who cer- tainly would have been present if it had been possible, consistent with otherarrangements madesome timp ago Another cause for regret was the inclement weather. But these were trifling matters as compared with what they had cause and reason to rejoice about. Although Mr. Arthur Crosfield was not present, Mrs. Crosfield, Miss Crosfield and Mr. George Crosfield were there— (applause)—which, he thought, showed a very sub- stantial amount of interest on the part of the family in the cause which was se near and dear to them and to the workers of the mission. Another cause for great I satisfaction was the fact that the works, the name of which had been a household word in Warrington for nearly three generations required illore room because there was more work to do, and that meant, to people in the district, grcater prosperity and larger and better employment. He hoped the?. would all live to see the day before ve!si long when that bigundertaking would be the biggest in Warrington and one of the biggest in the country. While the works had been growing their (the mission workers') cause had been growing. He did not say that there was any I necessary connection between the growth of the works and the growth of interest in the mission work, but it was a fact, the committee informed him that even if the works had not required the land on which the chapel stood, the congregation would have had to go somewhere else before very long to strengthen their stakes and widen their borders, because the accommodation in the chapel was becoming small for the number of people who attended. The rpresent was, therefore, a splendid opportunity to meet the • requirements of .the works on the one hand and the interests of the mission on the other. Reference had bees made to the fact that this cause was to be I carried on on non-sectarian and undenominational I lines. They heard a great deal about sectarianism I nowadays. They had had perhaps one of the biggest fights in Parliament, over what was called on the one I hand religion, but what was well known on the other ' hand to be sectarianism,that they had witnessed in their time, and the fight was by no means over. He was not , going to prophesy, but he ventured to have a very strong opinion that the condition of things which had permitted denominationalism as such to ride rough-shod over all that was fair and all that made for freedom, would not last a generation longer. -Whether that be so or not, if they hs,d a little less of denominationalism, a little less of what was called religion, and a little more of what was properly and well understood was Chris- tianity, they would all feel the better for it. If there was one feature more than another that was a marked feature in the influence and character of th.. late Mr. Crosfield, it was his cordial dislike of anything and everything which narrowed down religion to what might be called mere sectarianism and denominationalism He was broader, wider and bigger in his thoughts and ' ideas than that, and he (the speaker) remembered him saying that he preferred to be called not a Quaker, not a Churchman, but a Christian. (Applause.) His ideas were pretty much the same as the ideas of another great friend of his, and a life long companion—Mr. McMinnies Who he (the speaker) had often heard say that his ideas of religion were all bound up in the Sermon on the Mount. If they:could inculcate into the minds of children and young people at that Mission all that was taught in the Sermon on the Mount, they would have done a magnificent work. It' the result of the teaching the children received was to make them :hien and women in the best and truest sense of the term, men and women who would not yield to clamour on the one hand or to fear on the other, who would never consider expediency or personal comfort, but who would stand out if necessary against the whole world for what they believed to be right, they would have accomplished a grand work and a glorious mission. With all his heart he wished them every possible suc- cess in that undertaking and anything he could do in any way to further its interests, it would be a pleasure for him to do. (Applause.)

Councillor :LIMES EvANS addressed the gathering and said tb at among the many good things which the late Mr. Crosfield did for Warrington he perhaps never did a better work than when he built the mission at Bank Quay. After a reference to the late Mr. George Cros- field the speaker alluded to the results of the work at the mission and said he knew persons who had been greatly benefitted socially, morally, and religiously by the efforts of the friends at that place of worship. -In regard to the non-sectarian character of the teaching, the mission not only gathered in people and tried to reform them, but it found Christian employment ler all that came into touch with it. He felt that people were perhaps depending too much upon the ministerial element to-day. He thought that according to his ability every labourer in the vineyard should be employed. The talents of all the members of a Churcsh would thus be brought into use and he thought that if ever they were to obtain efficiency in church work they certainly ought to obtain it in that direction. He wished , the mission more abundant success than it ' had attained in the past, and he was sure that if the members continued to gather the chil- dren together every Sunday and instil into their minds principles that would have effect in after life and tend to higher and better conditions of citizen- ship, something would be achieved. He was pleased to learn that there was a Band of Hope organization in ,connection with the mission, where the young people would be taught habits of sobriety. That was one of the great needs of the day. He endorsed the opinion of Lord Rosebery that if we did not get hold of the drink traffic it was going to get hold of us. It was not so much the fiscal policy as the drink question that we needed to interfere with. England's drawback to-day was not merely its want of money and work, but its waste. (Applause). Mr. T. DALE moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Mrs.Crosfield, Captain Crosfield,and all who hadiassisted in thej ceremony, or sent letters regretting inability to attend. They were very much indebted to the hon. secretary far the trouble he had gone tc in making the arrangements, and to the band for their valuable services. He (the speaker) had been identified with the mission for over twenty years, and the old ml salon had sacred memories for him. He hoped God would continue to bless their cause. (Applause). Councillor BURTON seconded, and referred to previous ceremonies of a similar character in which he had taken part. The late Mr. Crosfield always responded readily and willingly to appeals that were made to him on behalf of deserving causes, and not only helped them financially but showed sympathy with the work. He (the speaker) was very glad that Messrs. Crosfield's works were so prosperous because it was a very good sign for the prosperity of Warrington. Inconclusion Councillor Burton alluded to ths need for young men to help in the mission work. The motion was heartily agreed to, Mr. George Wall- ington, who put it to the meeting, remarking that he took part in the laying of the foundation stone of the old mission and had rejoiced in its success during the past thirty years. He hoped it would go onand prosper in increasing ratio. (Applause.) In responding the CHAIRMAN said Mrs. Crosfield took a keen and earnest interest in everything that ap- pertained to the mission and school and she had shown it in more ways that one. She would, he knew, continue to show that interest. Exactly the same remarks ap- plied to Miss Crosfield and Mr. George Crosfield. What- ever the late Mr. Crcsfield himself wished in regard to that mission, they could take it for granted from his I knowledge of the family that the same wishes obtained in the heart of each one of them. He was sure the occasion had been a very interesting and agreeable one. They had that day entered upon a new era in their history which they believed woulA be a brighter and more prosperous one than any which had preceded it. A great deal depended upon themselves. They had perhaps depended to some extent necessarily for financial aid upon those who were better' off in this world's goods than themselves. It was quite possible that they might have to do a little more for themselves in the future than they had had to do in the past. He I did not think they would misunderstand him when he said that if a man's religion was not worth paying for it was not worth having. (Applause.) There were branches of the Christian Church where heavy contribu- tions were not often required, but in all forms of Non- conformity—he said it with gratitude and pride—they had got to payand it was a privilege to do so. (Hear,hear.) He hoped they would not forget that in the training of the youngsters. Let them understand that, holding a proper view upon every question appertaining to their own religious faith, they must be prepared to pay for it and assist in spreading it by every means in their power. (Applause). The hymn "Great God, Thy watchful care we bless " having been sung, Councillor BROUGH pronounced the Benediction and a selection by the band concluded the interesting proceedings.

An adjournment was then made to the site of the new WARRINGTON SECONDARY SCHOOL. I chapel and, in drizzling rain, the ceremony of laying the foundation stone was performed. i - Mrs. Henry Roberts handed a handsome silver trowel to Captain 6. R. CROSFIELD, who, after going through the usual ceremony, said "1 cteclare this stone to be well and truly laid, in the Name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost."

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE REV. F. A SCREETON.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF THE REV. F. A SCREETON.

At Christ Church, Latchford4 on Sunday evening the Vicar (the Rev. F. A. Screeton) made an announcement which was received with regret by the congregation— that he will shortly leave the parish to take charge of St. Thomas's Church, Hyde. During the six years that he has laboured in the parish the rev, gentleman has gained the esteem of a large 'circle of friends who will heartily wish-him success in his new sphere of work. Under his care the church has made great progress and quite recently was enlarged in order to accommodate the increased congregation. In announcing his impendini, departure the Vicar said :—" I daresay most of you Illowthat the Bishop of Chester has offered me the benefice of St. Thomas'a Hyde, and, after very careful consideration I decided that there was no other course open to me but to accept it. You all know very well that that decision would he made with anything but elated feelings. Indeed,' have felt very sad and depressed ever since. It is now more than six years since I first came here under the 'cloud of a great sorrow, and with the expectation of staying only a very short time. You were kind enough to take all this into account; I cannot tell you what a trial it vias to leave Chester. I never thought that any other place could be to me what St. Barnabas', Chester had been, but in the course of these six years, with its many friendships, its happy ministry, and pleasant associations, Christ Church has grown very dear to me. We have always worked well together. Of course, it is impossible that ever single thing would work smoothly when one has to deal with so many different dispositions and temperaments, but it has always been my wish to • be on the best terms with everybody. That we have worked harmoni- ously together is evidenced by the general progress of church work in the parish in every department, and it cannot but be a proud pleasure to me to know that in the enlargement of the church last year you have something which will ever remain a witness to the work and progress of the church here during the years I have been with you. There are other improvements already contemplated I should like to have seen carried out, but Which must be left to my successor. I am not unaware who he is likely to be. He is an old friend, I know his worth, and I hope for the sake of the parish he will accept the offer which has been made him. I find it hard to root myself up from congenial soil, but it seems to he my plain and obvious duty. Whatever betide and whatever the future may have in store for me I shall never forget Christ Church, Latchford, nor cease to ask that God's blessing may est upon you and yours."

div.head: Appointment of the Teaching Sta7f.
div.p: Appointment of the Teaching Sta7f.
A meeting of the School Management Sub-committee was held at the Technical Institute on Tuesday for the purpose of appointing the teaching staff for the new secondary school.

There were 106 applicants for the position of head- master, eight of whom were invited to appear before the comtnittee for final selection. The salary is £250 a year, and candidates had to be between 25 and 40 years of age. They had also to have had experience in a secondary day school (a) and be graduates of a British University. The successful candidate was Mr. Alexander Gow, B.A. (Cantab), B.Sc. (London), F.C.S., who has just completed three years' residence at Cambridge University. Mr. Gow was educated at Hill-street Elementary School, Crewe. He holds a first-class certificate in part one and a double first in part two of the Natural Science Tripos. He was trained two years at the Borough-road Training College, Isleworth where he obtained first class in certificate examination. For three years he was science master at the County High School, Isleworth, and had the organisation and control of one polytechnic, one art school and four subsidiary schools. He is 34 years of age. For theposition of chemistry master, which is worth £l4O ayear,there were 20 applicants.Of the three applicants who were selected to appear before the committee, Mr. Frederick William Rixon, M.Sc., Ph.D., was appointed Mr. Rixon, who is 23 years of age, was educated at the Owens College for five years, and for two years at the ' University of Giessen. He formerly taught at the Denton Technical Evening Classes, and has just returned from Giessen.

Mr. Richard Henry Albery, B.Sc., was elected out of 11 applicants for the position of physics master at a salary of £l4oa year. He was trained at the University Day Training College, Liverpool, where he has been up to the present post graduate research student and assistant demonstrator in physics at Liverpool. He is 24 years of age. Mr. John Lthony Buckley, MA., Wigan Grammar School, wasappointed out of 17 applicants assistant master in the secondary day school at a salary of £l2O a year. He is 21 years of age. Twenty-eight applications were received for the posi- ,tions of assistant mistresses for general subjects at salaries of £.llO each. The successful candidades were Miss Elizabeth Frost who was for three years pupil teacher at Widnes Day School, and at present assistant mistress at Goodrich-road Higher Grade School, E. Dulwich, London, and Miss Margaret B. Morton, graduate at St. Andrew's University, who has taught at Burnley, Upper Norwood High School, and Merthyr Advanced Girls' School.

Of the 28 applicants for the position of mama instructor, at a salary of £llO Mr. Henry 0. Armstrong, chief instructor of manual training at Southend-on-Sea School Board, received the appointment. He is 27 years of age.

div.head: Thelwall Nuisance.
div.p: Thelwall Nuisance.

Sir,—We have arrived at a very curious phase of this -nuisance, for in your report at the Runcorn Rural Dis- trict Council meeting the strong prejudices of the ' Chairman and others are strangely manifested---,Even , poor Mr. Tighe's letter was passed over, though it ' clearly proved 'that Professor Delepine's conclusions respecting the outbreak of diptheria at Thelwall, were shown to be *ithout foundation.l Admiral %Jones-Parry protested about the mysterious and irregular way the report had been obtained; but the Council decided to pay far the same, although they have no legal 'right to do this and any members signing the cheque for pay- ment can be surcharged with the amount. Things have been carried with a very high • hand, but the public reading your report can quite see there is something somewhere'wrong, and when the tale comes to be told in all its full reality I am. afraid -many things will be brought to light, which will not bring • credit to this authority. Alasl the nuisance still continues.—Yours faithfully, R. A. -NAYLOR.

Castle Hotel, Conway, August 20th, 1903. -- Magistrates and tile Vaccination law. Sir,—At Liverpool the other day the following little colloquy took place between the stipendiary magis- trate and an applicant fora vaccination exemption order The Magistrate told applicant that he was not satisfied with his eansoience. Applicant: Can you tell :me what will satisfy you, then? The Magistrate:—No, I cannot. The Act of Parliament does not say, I must satisfy you. You must satisfy me. Applicant: Then what am I to do ? The Magistrate:—Th.ere are plenty of other magistrates in Liverpool. if you can find any soft enough to agree with. There may be some cranks among them. Here then it is quite clear that, in the opinion of this sapient gentlemen, the character of this vaccination Act is such that only " softs " and "cranks " will administer it. Now this certainly cannot be over flattering to the collective wisdom of the "Strongest Government of 'Modern Times" which passed it, noryet to these magistrates who do administer it according to its•spirit and intent. However much an Act of Parlia- ixtent may conflict with personal bias, it is hardly con- ceivable that one appointed and paid for its administra- tion would thus so flagrantly float and defy it did he mot feel assured-of- encouragement from those quarters whence a rebuke ,would be more appropriate. As nothing is more certain than that the complete emanci- pation fronythis vaccination tyranny has to be won at the polls it is hoped that at the coming generaleleetion -this question *lll—as its importance deserves—be made the'paramount one, and votes given only to those can 41idates pledged to assist in the work of ridding the Statute book of this obnoxious law.—Yours faithfully J. WEST. Bradford-on- *von, August 18th, 1903.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.
SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT ON " COLONIAL PREFERENCE AND THE TAXATION OF FOOD."

Sir William Harcourt in a letter addressed to the "Times "urges -thaE the materials for forming a judg- ment on Air. Chamberlain's policy are now perfectly accessible and sufficient. The taxation of food is the keystone of the policy-, since without it there can be no colonial preference. If it is decided that food is not to be taxed by a protective duty, itis impossible to apply such a duty to any other industry. Colonial pre- ference and the taxation of food is a very plain, simple, ' and intelligible issue, not to be confounded by potter- ing inquiries and evasive manceuvres." Let us be told, he says, whether this policy is accepted or rejected by the responsible Government, and the nation will know how to deal with it.

div.head: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN MESSRS W. P. RYLANDS AND A. H. CROSFIELD.
div.p: THE CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN MESSRS W. P. RYLANDS AND A. H. CROSFIELD.

Mr. CHARLES E. PARKER writes:— The interesting correspondence that has been appall-- lag from week to week in your paper between the above gentlemen has been conducted with such ability, on both sides, that it is a matter of regret to many that it appears to have now closed. Such letters are educa- tional in the highest degree, and will help all who are desirous of arriving at a right conclusion in regard to the great controversy of the hour. My object in adding anything is simply to call Mr. Rylands' attention to what appears to me to be a mani- fest error in his last letter. In striving to correct some figures of Mr. Crosfield's he appears somehow to have fallen into a mistake in regard to the imports into , Australia, which if I ant right,. sustains the position taken up by Mr. Crosfield, viz., that the amount of foreign trade with the Colonies which we could exploit by aid of Preferential Tariffs is comparatively very small. Mr. Rylands is correct in saying that in 1900 we exported to Australia, 21,i millions, except that in addition to this we re-exported to this Colony two millions of foreign and colonial produce. The Austrivlian figures give twenty-six millions for that year, but probably the difference is accounted for by the added value through freights. Bat the total Australian imports for that year were only about 38 millions, thus leaving twelve millions as the proportion from our colon- ies and foreign countries. I think if Mr. Rylands will look into the matter he will find that the statement of Mr. Crosfield, that we already- hold 71 per cent of the Australian trade is correct. I do not know how Mr. Rylands arrived at his figures except it be that he in- cluded the international trade of the now 'combined 'Australian States. This.would be like including the trade between England, Scotland, Ireland, and Wales when speaking of the imports into Great Britain. I think Mr. Rylands will acknowledge that the trade we could exploit is not nearly so great ashis last letter in- dicated and that Mr. Crosfield was perfectly right in reducing it to its real dimensions. A word about India. ,Thisidependency takes from foreign countries in manufactured and partly manu- factured goods, roughly seven millions. This is the gross amount of trade our manufacturers could exploit. Out of this seven millions there will have to be a very large deduction made for,first,lgoods we could net make because the raw material is too costly to bring from the east and send back again in a manufactured form. Secondly, goods that are of eastern manufacture (mostly handmade) such as the silk goods of China and Japan. Andthirdly goods of cheap low,. priced make that it would not pay British labour to waste its time over. I very much doubt if preferential tariffs would be able to divert three millions to Br tish manufacture. The Indian tariffs are necessary for revenue. :If they are lowered for British goods how is India trebe re- 1 couped ? The basis of Mr. Chamberlain's plan is a preference on food stuffs coming into Great Britain in exchange for a preference on British manufactures going into the Colonies. But India only sends us in food stuffs, tea and rice, and in these two articles they have no foreign competitors. Were we to give India a ,pre- ference in these it would do her no good because there are no similar foreign goods to shut out. Mr. Rylands says it is un-English to be afraid of difficulties. Surely it is equally un-English to adopt unworkable illconsidered schemes. If this England of ours from a natural Conservatism, has been slow in resorting to the experiments in legislation which other countries have tried, it has this in its favour that it has not had to go back after finding out by bitter experi- ence its mistakes. Our progress may have been slow but it has been steady and sure and every forward step has been well considered and none have had to be retraced.

div.head: DISASTROUS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DISASTROUS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.
Cabinet Works Destroyed.

In the early hours of yesterday moining a disastrous fire broke out at the works of Messrs. J. M. Greenhalgh and Company, cabinet makers and upholsterers, in , Church-street, Warrington. About ten minutes to three o'clock, Mr. George Archer, a compositor was walking along Church-street when he heaid a crackling noise, accompanied by a smell of burning timber. On reaching Messrs. Greenhalgh's premises he found them well ; alight and hastened to give the alarm to P.C. Hamblett. Fortunately a cyclist Caine along and he conveyed the news to the Fire Engine Station with all haste. Pending the arrival of the brigade, Mr. Archer and P.C. Hamblett jumped over the wall adjoining the premises and with some difficulty succeeded in rescuing a valuable horse from the stable. The brigade arrived with great promptitude with reel, escapes, ladders, Sze. The engine "Captain "followed immediately afterwards and was succeeded by the "Major." The men quickly got to work under the sapervision of Superintendent Turner and Deputy- Superintendent Turner, and in a short space of time the two steamers and 14 hydrants were at work. The flames shot up to a great height and illuminated the district. The inflammable nature of the material made it impossible to save the burning buildings, andfthe firemen chiefly directed their efforts to the work of preventing the flames from spreading to adjoining works and to a stack of timber in the yard. The..works in the immediate vicinity include those belonging to Messrs. J. Mounfield and Sons, Mr. E. Forshaw, and Messrs. T. Locker ann Sons, Ltd. Owing to the situation of Messrs. Green- halgh's works it was with some difficulty that the fire was confined to the works themselves, and four or five hours elapsed before the fire was under control. For- tunately the wind was blowing from the south-west . which wasa great help to the firemen and they suc- ceeded in preventing any serious damage being done to adjoining premises. The cabinet shop, saw mills, polishing rooms and drying shed i of Messrs. Greenhalgh and Co. were completely wrecked and some valuable machinery and tools were destroyed as well as some finished goods arid a furniture van. The only portion of the stock and plant saved from the wreckage was an overhead crane and some piles of valuable hard wood. Our representative saw Mr. Greenhalgh last evening but he stated that it was impossible to form even an approximate estimate of the damage which was very considerable. Fortunately the premises and stock are fully insured. Many of the employes suffered the loss of valuable tools. Most of the articles were insured and the firm intend to replace those which are not , covered by insurance.

div.head: DOUBLE DROWNING FATALITY.
div.p: DOUBLE DROWNING FATALITY.
A Boy's Fatal Gallantry at Latchford.

Peculiarly distressing are the circumstances surround- ing the death of two Latchford boys who were drowned in the Bridgewater Canal on Wednesday evening. It appears that threa boys named John Elandford Corbett, aged nine, son of Mr. Jos,ph Rowland Corbett, of 9. Belmont-avenue' Latchford: John Hodgeson Wilson, aged 10, son of Mr. William John Wilson, G. Lyon- street; and a companion!named Acton, were playing on the wooden turn-bridge which spans the Bridgewater Canal near Black Bear Bridge when Corbett fell into the water Wilson at once divested himself of his coat and jump- ing into the canil made a gallant attempt to rescue his friend.. Unfortunately both boys sank and before assist- ance was forthcoming they were drowned. The bodies were recovered shortly after by a man named Joseph Lowe, a Runcorn boat captain. Artificial respiration was applied for nearly an hour, but unfortunately with- out avail, and Dr. Smith, who was summoned to the spot, pronounced life to be extinct. The bodies were removed to the homes of the, parents. Mr. Corbett is very well known in Warrington, having recently con- ducted .a series of mission services in the Parr Hall. Much sympathy is felt with him and with Alr. Wilson in their painfully sudden bereavement. It is only a few weeks ago that the boy Wilson was success- ful in saving a boy from . drowning in a pit. at Latch- ford and he was shortly to receive the Royal Humane Society's award for his gallantry. It is indeed sad to think that at so early an ago his life should have been I sacrificed in an attempt to save another.
VIE INQUEST.
THE CORONER AND WILSON'S BRAVERY.

Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, yesterday conducted an inquiry into the circumstances attending the deaths of the two boys. Mary Wilson, wife of William John Wilson, store- , keeper, of 6. Lyon-street, said her son John Hodgeson , Wilson was 10 years of age. He left home at about one o'clock and went to Wash-lane school. She next saw him at 7.30 when he was brought home dead. • The Coroner: Is it true that your boy saved a boy's life some time ago? Witness replied in the affirmative. Mr. Wilson, father of the lad, in answer to the I Coroner, said his son rescued a boy from drowning in a pit near the Canal on August Ist. A paper had been received from the Royal Humane Society for him to fill up. He understood his son was to receive some I recognition of his services, but he did not .know what the award was. Detective Barlow, Coroner's officer, said he was in- formed that Wilson was to have been presented with a silver medal at Wash-lane schools in recognition of his bravery. He did not know what the Humane Society intended doing. • Mrs. Corbett, wife of Joseph Corbett, an evangelist, said her son was 9 years of age. He left home about. one o'clock on Wednesday and was brought home dead about 7.30 the same day. George Acton, 10 years of age, son of Joseph Acton, 2, Lyon-street, said that at 4.30 on Wednesday afternoon he and the deceased boys were playing near the old wooden tumbril:lige on the Bridgewater Canal. Wilson was in the act of turning the bridge, and Corbett tried to itunp on to it, but missed and fell into the water. Wilson at once took off his jacket and jumped into the canal, but both boys were drowned. Witness informed a batman of what had occurred, and he recovered the bodies with a boathook. There was no one near the bridge at the time of the accident except witness and the other two lads. The Vorernan (Mr. Lake) said this was not the first accident that had occurred at this particular spot. P.C. Hardy, stationed at Latchford, said the bodies had just been re.:.,•o7ered when ha appeared on the scene Artificial respiration was resorted to, but when Dr. Smith saw the boys he pronounced them to be dead. If a boy once got into this water, which was dirty and deep, he had little chance of getting out again, as the sides of the canal were steep. The boatman was about 100 yards away at the time. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death." In the case of Wilson it was recorded that he was drowned while attempting to save the life of Corbett. The Coroner was asked to convey the sympathy of the jury to the bereaved parents. The Coroner (addressing the parents of the deceased boys) said : The jury, in returning their verdict, want MO .to convey to you their sympathy in the loss you have sustained Of course I don't know you as well as the jury, but I join in the expression of sym- pathy. It is to be regretted that Wilson lost his life. I should feel proud if a lad of mine had lost his life under circumstances such as these, where he had saved a life and lost his own in trying to save another. should be proud to be the father of such a lad. The parents thanked the Coroner and jury for their expressions of sympathy.

div.head: MORE ABOUT THE COBDEN CLUB.
div.p: MORE ABOUT THE COBDEN CLUB.
THE HOUSE OF LORDS.
BY GEORGE GREENWOOD.

That the veto of the House of Lords must either be greatly restricted or abolished altogether is a proposi- tion which for many years past has always been greeted with cheers at Liberal meetings throughout the country.
Resolutions to that effect_liave been again

and again unanimously carried-at the annual meetings of the National Liberal Federation. Such resolutions usually stand in some such form as the following: "That this Council maintains its firm conviction that Parliament will never be really representative and efficient until the House of Lords is rendered powerless to prevent th,) passing of any bill deliberately ap- proved by the House of Commons, by depriving the Upper House of the power of veto which it at all times possesses, but which it only uses to defeat or mutilate legislation passes through the House of Commons by a Liberal Government." (Carried at Nottingham, March, 1900.) There is, therefore, practical unanimity as to the object in view. The difficulty arises when it is asked how that object is to be achieved; bat unless all this tall talk is.merely to end in smoke it is, I conceive, high time that Liberals should consider the subject in a practical light, with the view of arriving at some plan of operations which may be carried into effect when the party once more comes into power—an event which, as we confidently hope, is not far dis- tant. For it is certain that if the veto Of the Lords be left intact, the next Liberal Government, should they attempt—as they must attempt—to pass measures of far-reaching democratic reform will find that they are again, to quote Mr. Asquith's historic expression, merely "ploughing the sands of the seashore. It may be well, before we pass on, to consider for a moment the constitution of the House of Lords._ In

1902 that House had upon its rolls the names of five hundred and ninety "Lords Spiritual and Temporal," though, except when some great Liberal measure is to be opposed, comparatively few of these august personages think it necessary to attend in the Gilded Chamber. The" Lords Spiritual "are the two Arch- bishops and] wenty-four Bishops of the Established Church. No more striking example could be given of the patient (not to say pusillanimous) endurance of the British people than the fact that these dignataries of the State Church should still be endowed for life with a vote in this legislative assembly. Needless to say, they have, with very few exceptions, always.shewn themselves the creatures of privilege and prejudice, and the bitter opponents of all measures of enlight- ened progress and reform. The "Lords Temporal" include, besides four "Princes of the Blood" and four "Law Lords" who hold life peerages, forty-four so-called " representa- tive " peers, viz., sixteen peers of Scotland and twenty-eight peers of Ireland. The " representative " Beers of Ireland are elected for life- by the Irish nobility. The "representative" peers of Scotland are elected for one Parliament Only by the Scottish nobility. Thus Liberal Scotland and Nationalist Ireland are " represented " in the Hciuse of Lords by ' a solid phalanx of Tory Peers! The remaining peers are our "hereditary legislators." Now in feudal times it was no doubt natural enough that a great lord's title and privileges should' descend to his heir; but that this principle should be still in operation in this twentieth century, to the extent of mak- ing a man's seat in one of the legislative chambers hereditary, is • a flagrant instance of the Imanner in which the perverse ingenuity of man is apt 'to thwart nature by securing the survival of the unfittest. If a prosperous brewer who has ." made his pile."' and who has always voted with his party,wishes to be known for the remainder of his life as Lord Bung, there is perhaps no very strong reason why his desire should not be gratified. • But to endow hint with a seat for life in Parliament is preposterous; and to provide that such seat shall descend to his heirs, so long as his posterity shall endure, is mere midsummer mad- ness. If it were necessary .to have a Senate there might be a case for giving the successful lawyer, or even, the successful soldier, a seat in such assembly; but .as it is by no means improbable that the sons and grand sons whether of an Attcrney-General or an Army General, will be" fools or worse," to give a legislative vote to the posterity of these men" in tail male," simply be- cause' they have done us the honour to be born (not altogether a unique distinction), seems a sort of political Ism sequitur such as we should only expect to find in one of Mr. Gilbert's topsy-turvy comic operas.. For What can ennoble sots, or slaves, or cowards? Alas ! not all the blood of all the Howards ! I do not propose to give a catalogue of all the great and useful measures of reform which have been de- layed or indefinitely postponed owing to the prejudices and obstructive tactics of the House of Lords. Such an inquiry would far transcend the limits of the space allotted to .me. There are many historical and politi- cal works and pamphlets which will provide the : reader With full information on this branch of the subject. He might profitably begin with the year 1810, when a bill to abolish capital punish- ment for the. offence of shoplifting to the value of 55., which had been curried in the- Commons, was rejected in the House of Lords by at majority which included seven Bishops, not one pre- late being found to vote in favour of reforming a law so barbarous and so inhuman. If the student will carry his researches from that point down to the pre- sent time, he will find that his study, though certainly prolonged, has been by no .means uninstructive. As John Bright well said : " We nre always told that the Peers are necessary as a check. If that is so, I must say the answer their purpose admirably" ! And it is not only by rejecting bills that the Lords obstruct progressive legislation, for when they dare not reject their constant practice is to mutilate Liberal measures in such a manner as to deprive them of all vitality and of all real power for good. An instructive instance of this, and, at the same time, of the very different manner in which the Lords behave to a Tory as compared with a Liberal Government, is afforded by their conduct with regard to the question of Local Government for Ireland. "There was a bill," said Mr. Gladstone, speaking at Edinburgh in 1893, " for introducing municipal institutions into Ireland. The House of Lords threw out that bill year after year for, I think, six successive years ; and when they consented to its passing they cut it down in point of scope and in point of provisions in such a way that the municipal . institutions of Ireland, altogether better than nothing, are Such as England or Scotland would reject with contempt." Yet when the Tories, not long ago, brought in their Local Government for Ireland Bill, the House of Lords which has been well described as merely an additional wing of the Carlon Club, were as usual the Govern- ment's most obedient humble servants, They are, in deed, little more than a mere registering assembly so lowg as the Tories are in office. They killed the Liberal Employers' Liability Bill, but meekly took the Workmen's Compensation Act from the Tories. They strain at a Liberal gnat but swallow .a Tory camel. Who can doubt, for Instance, what -Would have been the fate of Mr. 'Wyndham's Irish Land Purchase Bill if it had been the work of a Liberal Government ? It would have been rejected with scorn and con- tumely. But this is not all:. ,- The Lords exercise their malign influence on Liberal bills before they are in- troduced into the House of Commous. A Liberal Minister, in framing any measure of reform, has al- ways the fear of the Lords before his eyes. He has to consider not what is best for the Country, but what he may have a chance of getting through the Upper House. Thus is many a good measure paralysed from its very birth. The evil eye "of the Lords rests upon the unhappy infant, and lo! it withers away! But no account of the Upper Chamber would be complete without Mr. Chamberlain's famous descrip- tion, delivered at Bingley Hall in 1881, which has now become the lo:u.s elasoicuo on the subject. "The House of Lords," said Mr. Chamberlain, "for one hundred' years has never contributed one iota to popular liberties, or done anything to advance the common weal; and during that time it has protected every abuse and sheltered every privilege. It has denied justice, and delayed reform ; it is irresponsible without independence, obstinate without courage, arbitrary without judgment, and arrogant without knowledge." This is, indeed, a somewhat exaggerated description' quite after the manner of a politician who is always thinking more of the effect which his words will pro- duce than of the obligations of strict veracity ; but, as Mr. Gladstone said when quoting the passage at Edinburgh in 1893 : "It is a statement in whicli I painfully acknowledge there is much substantial truth." Nevertheless, Liberals should beware of proposals to reform the House of Lords. t No doubt the exclusion of the Bishops, and a systent by which more truly representative Peers might be elected for Scotland and Ireland, would do something to improve the Upper House. But a -reformed House of Lords would be a strengthened House of Lords. A reconstituted Second Chamber

based upon a brand-new statute of the Imperial Par- liament, would, in the event of a conflict with the popular Chamber (a contingency certain to occur sooner or later), be in a position to assert its rights ia opposition to the will of the people with a strength,, and confidence which our " hereditary legislators can neither feel nor claim. The only fact, thing, in which we can contemplate with any approach to satis- faction in the House of Lords as it at present e:cists is its essential•weakness, due to its unrepresentative character and the obvious absurdity of the hereditary system. To give new title-deeds to the House of Lords can never be .an article of the Radical pro-

gramme. But, it may be asked, " Why all this talk about reform? What we want is the abolition of the House of Lords ! " I will not stop here to discuss the ques- tion of the necessity of a Second Chamber. For the present it seems to me a sufficient answer to the pro- posal to "abolish the House of Lords" that it can 011-15-- be effected either by the willingness of the Peers ta "commit suicide," by passing a measure for their own destruction, or by a revolution. Neither of these, solutions seems at present to be within the range nt. practical politics, however desirable such proposed reform may be. A. more practical solution of the difficulty seems t°' be the limitation of the veto of the House of Lords- Thus, it might be provided by Act of Parliament that the rejection by the Peers of a bill sent up to them b.Y. the Commons should only be operative for .a limited period, after which, in the event of the same measure., again receiving the sanction of the popular chamber, should become law, Whether or not the Peers should be waling to agree to it. But how, it will be asked, are the Peers to be in- duced to pass such an Act, so seriously limiting their powers? Here we have an invaluable precedent i 3 the course taken by Lord Grey in 1831 in order to coerce the Lords into accepting the Great Refortn Bill. Lord Grey obtained from King William IV. his written authority to create as many. new Peers 35' might be necessary to secure a majority for tile measure in the Upper House. The mere threat vc3,-! sufficient, for rather than see their "Gilded Chamber flooded by a number of upstart Peers the Lords go way, and the Reform Bill became law. It has been; suggßsted, by a high legal authority in the Liberal. party —and the suggestion seems worthy of verY serious consideration—that the Prime Minister designate of the next Liberal Government, whoever be may be, should refuse to form a Cabinet unless he be armed with a similar authority from the .Sovereie, viz., an authority to create, if it should be requisite so many new Peers as may be necessary to secure the. passing of a bill to limit the veto of the Reuse et Lords. This done, the snake if not killed would 3t least be scotched; and no measure which the Commons were determined to pass into law could be. long delayed by the obstruction of a few irresp)usible and unrepresentative Peers. We should no longer be " ploughing the sands of the seashore." The problem is no doubt a difficult one, but it obvious that some decisive action must be taken, and it is surely time that Liberals should endeavour tc' arrive at some clear conception of what ought to bue done, for, as Mr. Glivlstone said, in. the last sPeec which he delivered in Parliament "The question is whether the judgment of the House of Lords is merely to modify, but is to annihilate the whole Nor' of the House of Commons, work which has been per- formed at an amount and sacrifice of time, labour, convenience, and perhaps health, totally unknown. t° the House of Lords." This reform, then, was solemnly committed afla commended to us by our great Leader;and this,sureli is the first and most important question villic Liberals have to consider. For the limitation of the veto of the House of Lords is the condition precedent to all efficient democratic legislation. GEORGE GREENWOOD.

The question was asked at a social gathering 0E politicians the other day who was the best informed member of the House of Commons, and the .auswera, were unanitnous--Sir Charles Dilke. In the talk about the Colonies and the Zollverein question, on (?:--'f remembers that Sir Charles Duke led the way study of British Imperialism years ago in political classic," G !eater Britain." When the Art totror or the Navy is discussed, Sir Charles Mike is jot' forefront as the most prominent member of the Sersl,;l, Committee. If the conversation is about the cordiale with France, one is reminded that it was who. as Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, tinted the Commercial Tre2ty with France in 18t3 upon which the close relations of the two nationslOc been established. In foreign affairs, indeed, nothing is alien to 11; His opinion is Sought by jeurnalists abroad on 9.. problems of the Far East with the same eageraesr that the leading American reviews apply to him f° articles on American policy. . h On Labour matters at home his counsel is —eof equally weighty. He is a marvel in the elucidation statistics, and thus fully maintains the reputation ,e , acquired as President of the Local Government Boaro. 1 But what is most surprising is that with all the._ studies he maintains his vivacity and interest l'ir essentially literary affairs. He is the best Frelleto scholar in the House of Commons, and dips also ill" German philosophy. As proprietor of the Athentran he exercises an active control over the. reviews, 911 to. often, when the subject is one which he wish° have specially treated, he writes the review hirlse b`it Sir Charles Dilke is close on sixty years of ages finds recreation in fencing, and sculling. The special article which he will contribute to columns next week is'entitled "COLONIAL PREFERPCS,thr MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S SCHEME." He deals witll subject in a most exhaustive manner. The death occurred with painful suddenness at Warrington.—M. Hickling, St. Elphin's Clergy Harrogate on Saturday of Mrs. Higginbottom, wife of Daughters' School. Mr. Charles Higginbottom, of Ferndale, Grappenhall- road, Stockton Heath. The deceased lady, who was in her 47th year, wa,4 in the town shopping at about eleven o'clock in the morning when she fell to the, ground in a fainting c mdition. It was seen that her illness was serious, and she was at once picked up and conveyed to the Infirmary. She remained uncon- scious until ten o'clock in the evening when she passed away. She and her husband had only 'arrived at Harrogate on the previous day. Mr. Higgiubottom was not with his wife at the time she fell, but as soon as he ascertained where she was he proceeded to the hospital, and was distressed to find her in such a serious condition. By a happy coincidence the nurse whose duty it was to attend to her-was Miss Longdin, a daughter of the Warr ngtou Borough ... ' airvey-or. Much sympathy has been expressed for Mr. Higgiti- bottom (who is the secretary for Messrs. Waring and Co., tanners, Winwick-road) in his very sudden bereavement. GIVE THEM A TRIAL.—ALF, TAYLOR'S wonder- ful boots for everybody. ' Large Profit on Cabbages. At the 'Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen. Rowlands, K.C., an action was heard in which john Thamas, licensee of the Parr Arms, Grappenhall, sued Jonathan Broad- hurst, greengrocer, Bostock-street, for Lifer cabbages - sold.—Mr. Arthur Browne, who represented the plaintiff, stated that although the amount of the claim , was small, the plaintiff was determined to make the i defendant pay the money, and thus set an example to lothers. The defendant was a greengrocer, and he met . the plaintiff and asked him if he had any cabbages to sell. Mr. , Thomas said -he had, and shortly . afterwards, a man came with the defendant's cart to Grappenliall and agreed to take a load of cabbages at 7d. a dozen. The man stated that he had Mr. Broadhurst's author- ity to buy the cabbages and that Mr. Broadhurst would pay the plaintiff the first time he saw him. The defendant saw the plaintiff some time after but dis- puted the bargain and said lie would only pay market price. The defendant's own man admitted: that he had sold the cabbages for Is. 6d. a dozen, which was equal to a profit of 120 per cent. —His Honour : What an enormous profit greengrocers can make.—John Thomas, the plaintiff gave evidence in support of Mr. Browne's statement, The defendant's man was allowed to choose his own stuff and as he left he said he would not sell one cabbage under 11,d. • HOW THE BLACK LIST OPERATES. A Warrington Example. The placing of John Wilfred Delooze, of Dudley-st., Warrington, upon the black-list appears to have had not the slightest effect upon that personage. Once more he appeared before the magistrates on Wednesday, charged with having been drunk and disorderly h.) Bridge-street at 1.45 the previous afternoon. Constable Baxendale said prisoner was very drunk and witness allowed a young man to take charge of him with the object of getting him home. Prisoner, however, broke away and acted in a disorderly manner. He picked up some fish from a cart that was standing in the street and was about to eat it when witness took him into custody. Superintendent Monagham said prisoner made his 31st appearance and had been before the Court for drunkenness seven times within twelve months. So recently as July 28th he was sentenced to 14 days' im- prisonment. Prisoner was now ordered to find a surety of £lO to be of good behaviour or go to prison for two months. CRICKET.
